1015.name: A broad, low-specificity feature that fires on content words in noun phrases, such as proper names, organizations, product and technical terms, and title-like phrases. It is strongest in formulaic or boilerplate text: website menus and buttons, affiliate disclaimers, attributions and bylines, license notes, regulatory listings and technical specs. Function words and running prose are largely ignored.

A diffuse, weak feature that fires on short content words, mostly nouns and name or term fragments. It is strongest on formulaic boilerplate, especially website UI and navigation text such as 'Post Your Answer', privacy/cookie policy, 'Press J to jump to the feed', keyboard shortcuts, 'Create Account', 'Popular' and 'user group'. Lower-level hits occur on code identifiers, headings and other key terms.

1032.name: Words or word-pieces starting with the letter "A" (either case), including names, acronyms, and ordinary words. Capitalized onsets and acronyms such as AME, AMZN and A. tend to be strongest, and continuation pieces are weaker.

Words or tokens beginning with the letter "A" (either case), such as names, nouns, code identifiers and fragments like "Am", "Ak", "Agency", "Action". Activation is strongest on the first, A-initial token, with weaker activation on the following subword pieces.

10376.name: The predicate right after a subject or relative pronoun (that/which/who/could/to) that describes how something behaves, performs or functions, e.g. 'scales up well', 'pays out large', 'tend to cook', 'utilize less power', 'deliver'. It is mostly verbs and their short complements expressing a characteristic capability or quality of the subject.

A weak, diffuse feature on predicate words right after a subject, mostly verbs and verb phrases (sometimes adjectives or adverbs) that describe how something functions, performs or behaves. Typical cases are "runs on", "handles", "measures", "outputs", "won't close right", "seem to work properly", "respond to" and "sold for". Activation is strongest on descriptions of a product's or entity's capabilities and performance.

10378.name: A weak, diffuse feature on the head nouns or final subword pieces of noun phrases. These are mostly concrete or technical nouns naming the substance, tool, carrier, medium or location involved in a described action or process. Examples include solvents, water, sand, mosquito, UAVs, vectors, instruments and arms. They often follow prepositions or verbs of means and location such as by, using, through, in, on and with.

Nouns (and occasionally phrases) denoting a carrier, holder, or medium through which something is held, conveyed, or delivered (carrier oil, envelope, backpack, vehicle, funnel, string for beads, setting, lap, rod, tick-borne, delivering a missile). Activations are weak and diffuse, peaking on 'carrier oil'.

1093.name: Diffuse, low-level activation over text with an Indian or South Asian flavor: Indian names and places (Patel, Sundaram, Sankaranarayanan, Satish, Hyderabad, Kautilya, Bhatt, Bollywood films). It fires most strongly on wordy, formal or non-native English phrasing typical of Indian English, such as "are of much significance", "I shall go on with", "paves a way to encourage", "give a lot of information on" and "As of now, the answer is No".

A diffuse, weak feature that fires on ordinary words and phrases in the middle of running clauses, mostly descriptive or instructional prose. It is strongest where natural-language explanation or instructions sit inside noisy, garbled, code-like or machine-generated text (e.g. "is displayed as per the value of", "Following are the sectors where we can add"). Activation is spread over spans of function and content words rather than tied to any specific token.

11014.name: Line breaks and other separator punctuation (newlines, periods, pipes, dashes, closing brackets) that end a short metadata field, most often right after a date or number in a header, byline or catalog listing, just before the next field or the main text begins.

Separator tokens (newlines, pipes, slashes, parentheses, periods) that immediately follow a date, year, timestamp or price in document headers and metadata, marking the shift from that metadata to the next field or the main text.

1106.name: A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires weakly across many tokens in varied contexts (prose, code, citations, headings). It is somewhat denser at the start of documents or sections, such as titles, bylines, headers, SQL/C++ code and citation lists, and on content nouns, proper-name fragments, and year/date pieces (e.g. '201', date commas). It has no clear single semantic meaning.

A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires broadly on unnatural, noisy, or machine-like text rather than on any one concept. Typical contexts are code snippets and markdown fences, numbered or enumerated lists, repetitive or degenerate sequences, garbled token salad, and fragments in non-Latin scripts. Activation is spread across many tokens in these contexts. It peaks on stray tokens, especially the bare space before a digit (e.g., '= 0', 'in 1'), plus odd items like 'python', 'order' in 'in order to', and oddly split words such as 'capt' or 'mitig'.

1120.name: Tokens at the very start of a document, the first few words of a title, header, or opening line (often split from the first token), plus lead-in material such as dates, versions, and section starts right after a title. Activation is highest on the first tokens and fades over the next few words.

Position-driven feature that fires on the first few tokens of a document or passage, regardless of content: titles, headings, code-block openers (```python, import, \documentclass), opening phrases of a sentence or question. Activation peaks on the first content token or two and fades over the following tokens, with weaker blips at nearby line breaks or punctuation.

11402.name: Fires where a just-mentioned term or entity is about to be defined, explained, or glossed: copulas and appositive starters like "is a", ", which is", ", or", ", a", "commonly known as", open parentheses before abbreviations or formulas, and dashes or quotes introducing a definition.

Tokens that start a definition or description of a just-named term, strongest on the copula ('is', 'which is', 'is a', 'an escape in') and on definition openers after a colon or parenthetical (e.g. 'Beech (Fagus) is', 'Threat: A simulated', 'Boolean is a value type'). Weak, scattered activation also appears on delimiters (parentheses, '=', colons, newlines) in code, lists and noisy synthetic text.

11422.name: The head noun or noun phrase that completes a prepositional phrase of setting or scope, most often after "in" (also "at", "of", "for", "from"). It names where, when or in what domain something holds: places (Bermuda, Uganda, your yard, the Pacific), contexts or sections (this section, the field, the modern world), times (that day, Saturday morning) and levels or uses (atomic levels, industrial use).

The final word (usually a noun) completing an adverbial phrase that sets the scope or context of a clause: a place (in the world, on campus, in the village, in Iraq), a time (on Monday, this month, so far, in the past), or a domain/group (academia and industry, her generation). These typically come at the end of a clause, right before punctuation or a continuation.

11487.name: Nouns for professional roles, especially legal representatives who act on someone's behalf. "Lawyer", "lawyers", "counsel", "attorney", "Defense" and "counsellor" activate most strongly. Weaker hits include other advisors and agents (broker, aide, ambassador, coach, doctor, advocate) and related words like "representing" and "advice".

Nouns for professionals who act on behalf of or advise a client, especially lawyers, attorneys and counsel, and also coaches, doctors, agents and providers. Activation is strongest for legal representatives tied to a specific party ("his lawyer", "plaintiff's counsel").

11696.name: A diffuse, weakly firing feature in expository technical/academic prose that triggers on ordinary function words, nouns and sentence punctuation rather than any specific token. It is strongest in mathematical or research-abstract language describing proofs, conjectures, relations and validation, e.g. 'conjectured', 'related by', 'empirical validation'.

A diffuse feature of expository, mostly academic or technical prose. It fires weakly on scattered content words, verbs and punctuation at clause boundaries. It peaks on predicate phrases that state a relationship between concepts, such as "are shown to be equivalent", "provides the connecting link", "belongs to" and "Now the" after a math expression. It responds most to the main verb or connective that carries an argument forward.

1181.name: Tokens inside descriptive or defining phrases that explain what a subject is, usually right after the subject, as in appositives (", a global leader in…"), "X is a…" definitions, parenthetical glosses and "such as" lists. Activation is highest on the article and the connecting prepositions (a, in, of, by, to) of encyclopedic, explanatory text.

A diffuse, mostly weak feature that fires on the content of expository or explanatory clauses: the predicate that defines or describes a term, concept or entity. Typical spans are "X refers to a shared, virtual space", "also known as web harvesting… is the process of", "a trust allows a grantor to transfer" and "which are common in traffic signs". The strongest activations fall in the middle of these definitional or descriptive phrases. Scattered function words in factual prose get only low activation.

11879.name: The word "void" in all its senses: emptiness or a gap left by absence ("left a void"), outer space or the abyss, invalidating something ("void the warranty"), and the C/C++/C# return type keyword, which activates most strongly. It also fires on "devoid". Rare weak activations on unrelated tokens are noise.

The word "void" (and "devoid") in every sense: the programming return/parameter type (strongest, especially "(void" and void in parameter lists), legal invalidity ("null and void"), emptiness or gaps ("fill the void"), and "devoid of" meaning lacking.

11938.name: Items inside sequences or lists of repeated or patterned elements, mostly numbers (e.g., comma- or space-separated values, grids, repeated digits, doubling series). It fires on later entries once a pattern is established and grows stronger as the sequence continues and becomes predictable.

Items within a repetitive list or sequence, mostly numbers or short codes (chords, letters, scores, citation numbers, lottery numbers, data values) separated by commas, dashes, slashes or newlines. It fires on elements in the middle or later part of the series, once the repeating pattern is established.

1204.name: Fires broadly on nearly every token at the very start of a document: titles, headlines, paper titles and author lines, headers, and the first sentences or code lines that follow. Activation is strongest on the title or headline and fades as the text continues. Very common words like "the" are often skipped.

A dense feature that fires on nearly every token near the start of a document. It appears across many kinds of content: code, headings, lists, math word problems and multilingual snippets. Activation is strongest in short, low-coherence or synthetic-looking text that repeats itself or echoes a title. It seems to track generic 'early, low-context document' text rather than any specific word or meaning.

1222.name: Negation words and constructions (not, n't, no, never, cannot, nobody, neither, without) and the words right after them that complete the negated predicate (e.g. "not necessary to", "never be a", "no reason to see"). Weaker activation on implicitly negative or limiting words such as few, low, avoid, restrictions and without.

Negation: words like "not", "never", "no", "nothing", "without", contractions such as "n't", and the words that follow inside the negated phrase (e.g. "not sure", "never made sense to"). Activation is highest on the negator and weaker on the rest of the phrase.

12313.name: Reports of casualties, damage, or other tallied outcomes: counts and quantities (numbers, "000", "dozens", "many, many") of people or things affected, along with death, injury, destruction, and loss words (died, killed, destroyed, injured). Activation is strongest in clauses like "387 people were...", "24 have sadly died", "teen killed". It is weaker for neutral number tallies and occasional stray tokens.

Counts and quantities of people or things affected by events, especially in news reporting: numbers and quantifiers (more than 50, dozens, thousands of, millions, many, some) and the nouns and verbs that go with them. It fires most strongly on casualty statements, e.g. 'six people were killed' or 'killed three people and injured hundreds'.

12578.name: A diffuse, low-strength feature that mostly fires on highly predictable tokens which complete a fixed phrase, collocation, compound term or split word, such as "top of page", "lingua franca", "state of the art", "par-agon" and "penetration depth". Its strongest activation is on an opening brace in code syntax.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on words inside an introductory or conditional clause that sets up the main statement. Typical frames are "If…", "For every…", "so for/from…" and "the higher the…, the more…". The activating word is usually the head noun or key word of that setup phrase, just before the clause resolves, as in "if it were O(n) then…" or "If a player draws any numbered card…".

1268.name: Diffuse, low-intensity activation on technical and procedural text that describes how something is done, such as the method, tool, or means used for a task. It is strongest in code comments (e.g. "//Use D3 to retrieve data", "De-allocate any memory here") and in instructional phrases like "how would we write this as", "have to use the HTTP Request node to interact with", "accessed in the same way" and "controlled through a".

Explanatory or instructional prose in technical/coding contexts, especially in assistant-style answers, code comments, and walkthroughs. It fires on phrases that describe how to implement, structure, or fix something ("you might add a call to", "use cmd instead", "here's how you could"), along with nearby section headers and transitions into code blocks.

12824.name: Mainly the subword fragment "oph" inside longer words (biopharmaceutical, nanophotonics, homophonic, fluorophore, Drosophila, cacophony). It also fires weakly on stray spaces and odd whitespace or encoding characters (non-breaking or zero-width spaces, mojibake like "Â", HTML entities, unusual quote marks) and on other mid-word fragments.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on tokens that are fragments of a longer unit whose continuation is unusual or split. It is strongest on a plain space just before a rare Unicode symbol (‡, non-breaking hyphen). It is moderate on mojibake bytes like "â" (from a garbled ’ or ™) and on daggers. It is weak on word-piece prefixes that start a multi-token word (oph, gly, hyper, aster), on zero-width spaces, and on URL or markup fragments.

13058.name: A weak, diffuse feature on document-opening boilerplate and metadata, such as titles, headers, datelines, timestamps, page and part numbers, citation and bibliographic fields, and the line breaks separating these header elements from body text.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on formal, official or bureaucratic document language, especially headers and metadata near the start of a text: press or news release labels, legislative titles ("AN ACT TO AMEND TITLE"), booking or arrest records, requests for proposals, filings, bug and issue numbers, datelines and timestamp separators. It also fires weakly on nouns in formal, report-like prose (record, request, submission, document).

13106.name: Document header and metadata text, chiefly bibliographic and publication details at the start of a page: journal volume, issue and number labels, dates, page counts and boilerplate such as 'Skip to content'. Activation is strongest on issue numbers, like the digit after 'No.' or 'Issue number' in a citation.

Bibliographic and publication-metadata tokens, mainly the month, day, year digits and issue numbers in citations of periodicals (e.g., "the Feb. 12, 2018 issue of", "(Nov-Dec 1985)"), plus words like "issue", "edition" and "magazine". Weaker activations land on other header or locator elements such as page and chapter numbers, breadcrumb "Home", and dateline punctuation.

1321.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires on the substantive, topic-carrying content of a passage: domain-specific nouns, noun phrases and their predicates (e.g., technical, medical, scientific, product or subject-matter terms such as 'deployment', 'vessel structures', 'psychosis', 'coursework', 'corrosive chemicals'). It spans whole clauses describing what is being done or discussed, peaking on key subject nouns and staying weak on generic framing words.

A broad, low-specificity feature that fires across spans of substantive content rather than on any particular word. It covers noun phrases and clauses that follow a verb or preposition, code statements and identifiers, and math expressions. Activation is strongest on the key content nouns of descriptive or definitional phrases (e.g. 'movie tickets', 'business partner's failure', 'education system's financial practices'). Connecting function words and boilerplate are mostly skipped.

1323.name: Sentence and clause boundaries: mostly the period that ends a sentence (plus closing parens, line breaks), and sometimes the conjunction or first word that opens the next clause ("But", "In", "and", "So"). Activation is strongest on the period right after a complete statement, just before a new sentence starts.

Clause and sentence boundaries. It fires mostly on the period (or comma, dash, or newline) that ends a full clause, especially a general statement, and sometimes on the first words of the next sentence ("We", "But", "It", "In").

13388.name: Language about hitting, shooting, or scoring against a target, plus related success measures. The strongest cases are sports performance and stats, such as batting averages, home runs, balls faced, boundaries, shot charts, landed punch combinations and scoring goals. Weaker cases cover accuracy, hitting a jackpot, missing, success rates and percentages.

Words about attempts, shooting, hitting and scoring accuracy, mostly in sports: shots, field goals, free throws, swings, hits, doubles, shooting percentages (FG%/FT%), and related success-rate stats. Weaker activations occur on general words about aiming, attempts, effectiveness or hitting a target.

13483.name: Words naming or describing statistical and empirical findings in scientific or analytical writing, such as reports of significance, effects, changes, trends, evidence and test results. It peaks on "significant"/"significantly" and p‑values after phrases like "showed", "were" or "found".

Words that express measured or evaluated magnitude, comparison, or outcome, especially statistical or quantitative judgments ("significant", "significantly", "statistically", "evidence of", "expectations", "exceeds", "over budget", "double-digit", "greater than", "disparity"). Activation is strongest for "significant" in a statistical sense.

1362.name: Tokens inside conventional, formulaic multi-word phrases and collocations (e.g. “have to do with”, “a long way to go”, “shadow of its former glory”, “years of experience”, “rather than”, “means that”, “contrary to what one might expect”). Activation is strongest on the predictable continuation words that complete a stock expression. Many of the marked tokens are the function words (prepositions, articles, auxiliaries) that glue these phrases together, rather than any particular content word.

Diffuse, low-intensity activations on common function words and generic connective phrases in fluent prose, such as prepositions, auxiliaries, determiners, and discourse markers like "also", "for example", "that suits", "not necessarily", "ensure", and "the ability to". The strongest hits are mid-sentence phrase heads that predict a common continuation; there is no clear topical content.

1364.name: Fires most strongly on non-English and non-Latin-script text split into subword pieces (Chinese, Arabic, Persian, Cyrillic, Vietnamese), and weakly on accented letters in European languages. It also responds faintly to unusual or rare tokens such as emoji, mojibake, long runs of table-of-contents dots, HTML table tags, LaTeX fragments and odd word fragments.

Non-English and non-Latin script tokens (especially Chinese characters, also Cyrillic, Japanese, Arabic, Amharic, odd Unicode) that show up in mostly English or code text, frequently as garbled or code-switched fragments. Activation peaks on the first character of a Chinese word. Weak firing also occurs on stray symbols, emoji and markdown separators.

13835.name: The token right after the opening word of a line, tag or label. It fires most strongly on HTML/shortcode attribute names that follow a tag name, such as type, id, src and http in <input type=, <button id=, <iframe src=, <meta http- and [slideshow_deploy id=. It fires weakly on the word after a leading header or label word, as in Posted March, Study Section and Import P, or after a command name, as in dig + and serverless logs.

Mostly weak, diffuse activations on the token right after a tag, label or heading word. The strongest cases are attribute names that directly follow a markup or shortcode tag name, such as id, url, name, alt and href in [caption id=,

13848.name: Weak, diffuse activations, mostly on subword pieces inside multi-token proper names, acronyms or technical terms. These are usually the first or middle fragment, as in "Gro|ys|man", "Craw|ley", "Cad|ie" and "T|GB". It tends to fire when the name or term was already seen earlier in the context, so the rest of the word can be predicted by copying. It also fires occasionally on ordinary nouns that refer back to an entity already mentioned.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires mostly on the head or first subword token of a specific referent. These are usually proper names of people, products, places or organizations (e.g., the first piece of a multi-token surname or brand), often an entity already mentioned or being referred back to. It also fires on a few ordinary nouns naming a specific object or entity.

1387.name: Words and name fragments beginning with the letter "h" (e.g. hence, health, hard, hydro, Hong, Hart, hospital). Activation lands on the h-initial token, usually at the start of a word, and sometimes continues weakly onto the following subword pieces.

Fires on tokens that begin with the letter "h"/"H" (e.g. hex, hooves, hours, high, headers, heights, Hidden, HMM, Here, His, Hyper-, .h), strongest on bare or capitalized H and short h-initial fragments, often in noisy code or garbled text.

14030.name: A diffuse, weakly activating feature with no single clear concept. It fires on content tokens that complete a predictable phrase or parallel structure, such as "rural compared with urban", "lost or stolen", "warm or cool" and "25 years in about 25 weeks". It also fires on the first piece of a proper noun or multi-token word (Kenyan, Makati, Bland-Altman, unbeatable). The strongest activation is on Wikipedia-style citation brackets such as "[4]".

A diffuse, weakly activating feature with no single topic. It fires on a word or subword inside a familiar multi-token unit, usually a noun or the start of a name, at a point where the continuation is highly predictable. Examples include fixed names and collocations ("US Food [and Drug]", "Edgar Allan [Poe]", "bed [and breakfast]", "Gust[avo]"), set phrases ("For example", "future generations", "warm and friendly", "Located in", "Dear"), and structured strings ("java[.lang]", "Twitter @", "GIVEAW[AY]").

14095.name: Completion tokens of multi-token names and specialized terms: the later subword or second word of proper nouns, acronyms and compound phrases (e.g. Go-Da|igo, Pal|ma, El Ni|ño, deep vein throm|bus, CGI|AR). Activation is strongest when the term is predictable, often because it already appeared earlier in the context.

Tokens that complete a named entity or a multi-token term, typically the final subword of a proper noun (person, place, brand, organization, or acronym), e.g. the end of a surname, place name, or company name that was split into pieces. These tokens are largely predictable from the preceding fragment. Activation is strongest on rare foreign or political names.

1432.name: A broad, low-intensity feature in informational, press-release-style prose about named organizations, companies, institutions and products. It fires on the words immediately following such names, especially the remainder of a multi-token name ("-Benz E-Class", "Labs, China"). It also fires on the descriptive clauses that state what the entity is, does or offers ("is responsible for the administration of", "have successfully developed and deployed", "is gathering the best"). Peaks fall on sentence boundaries and transitions (periods, line breaks, commas) within these entity-centered descriptions.

A diffuse, weak feature of formal expository or promotional prose, typical of AI-assistant or marketing writing. It fires on function words and structural tokens in definitional or descriptive passages ("X is a … that …", "Here's how…", "We design our services…"). It also fires on transitions such as line breaks, bullets, list numbers and header endings that introduce an explanation or definition. It is strongest at the start of a new descriptive sentence after a list or heading.

1453.name: Mostly word-internal subword fragments containing the short vowel 'i' (ib, imb, idip, ilit, isc, ique, ik, iox, ig, piez, mish, ric, sic, Vir/ilio), typically inside rare names, foreign words and technical terms that get split into several tokens. The fragment is usually the first or a middle piece of an unfamiliar word. Weaker hits fall on ordinary words and code identifiers with an 'i' (Pick, bit, PID, ZIP, kill, dip).

Tokens containing the vowel 'i' (or its equivalent in other scripts, e.g. Cyrillic 'и' or Persian 'ی'), most often short subword fragments in the middle of rare words, names, code identifiers or foreign text (e.g. 'ich', 'iss', 'ir', 'id', 'ik', 'is'). Activation is strongest on fragmentary i-syllables and weaker on whole common words that merely contain an 'i'.

1457.name: A diffuse, weak feature that fires on salient content noun phrases and named entities (people, places, companies, products, technical terms) in running prose. Proper names that act as a clause subject activate most strongly (Cicero, Ghent, Ukrainian, Apple, President). Activation sometimes spills onto the following verb phrase, relative clause ("who", "which") or trailing punctuation and newlines.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on content tokens such as nouns, noun phrases, numbers and code identifiers, especially items in lists or repeated structured patterns (number sequences, typedefs, key/value lines, 'coffee, tea, soft…'). It often appears in rambling, garbled or low-coherence text rather than marking any specific meaning.

14603.name: Weak, diffuse feature that fires on structural and boilerplate tokens in scraped web text, such as metadata separators (|, :, —, •), URL and domain fragments, page labels (Posts, Info, Results, "Failed" to load), and query-string parameters. It is strongest on attribute syntax inside HTML tags and shortcodes, like class="prettyprint lang" and id=. Occasional activations on ordinary prose words are low and uninformative.

A weak, diffuse feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires on tokens in formulaic, boilerplate or structured text (feed and page metadata, field labels and colons, recipe and manual phrasing) where the next token is highly predictable. Examples include word fragments mid-completion ("Sh"→ourly, "vac"→uums, "traff"→icked) and labels or colons just before a value.

14698.name: Binary operator tokens in math and code, mainly exponent operators (^, **, )^, ^{, ).^) placed just before a power such as 2. Weaker hits on other operators and casts (as, >=, -, /, <<) and on a few stray punctuation and whitespace tokens.

Exponentiation operators ("^", "^{", "**", ")^", Math.pow's comma) placed between a base and its exponent in math/code, especially polynomial terms like x^3. Weaker hits land on other binary operators (%, >=, >>) and on list-separating commas.

Exponentiation operators: the caret (^, ^{, ^\) or ** that raises a base to a power, especially right before an exponent like 2 or 3 in math, LaTeX or code. It also fires weakly on other operators and separators (/, ::, -, commas, periods, spaces).

1483.name: Fires on the final subword pieces that complete a word split across several tokens (e.g. bellig-erents, Repet-ition, non-perturb-ative, Crockp-ots), often spilling onto the next one or two tokens of the same noun phrase or name. It shows up mostly in technical terms, proper names, acronyms and version or code strings, and peaks on the token where the multi-token word is resolved.

A diffuse, weak feature. It fires most strongly on subword pieces that finish a word split across several tokens, such as "ude" in Jean-Claude, "ers" in man-agers, "ship", "eness", "ical" and the Cyrillic and Korean endings. It also often fires on the next one or two tokens that continue the phrase. This is common in noisy, garbled, code, multilingual or repetitive text, and it is not tied to any clear meaning.

14858.name: Titles, offices and role nouns for people (President, Minister, Prime Minister, CEO, director, chief, Gov., Queen, coach), typically right before a person's name. Activation is strongest for political leadership titles such as President, Prime Minister and Gov.

Titles of positions, offices and ranks (President, Prime Minister, Pope, Chancellor, Sheriff, Queen, director, mayor), firing most strongly on high-ranking political, religious or royal titles placed just before a person's name.

14893.name: A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires weakly on function words and punctuation at phrase or clause junctions, such as prepositions, conjunctions, articles, auxiliaries, commas and sentence or paragraph breaks. These are positions where the sentence is about to continue into a new constituent (e.g. 'is the ability to', ', which we have', 'and has').

A diffuse, weakly selective pattern with no clear semantic theme. It mostly fires on function words and clause connectors such as "to", "of", "that", "the", "was a", "yet you have a" and "with the". It also fires on sentence boundaries and paragraph breaks. These tokens tend to sit at points where a new clause or the main content of a phrase is about to begin.

15095.name: Tokens at boundaries within web-page boilerplate and metadata, such as the newline ending a field value (IDs, ISBNs, DOIs, dates, namespaces, "pages on⏎this wiki") just before the next label, and the word "navigation" in wiki "Jump to: navigation, search" headers. Generally marks where one structured, templated element ends and the next begins.

Weak, diffuse feature that fires on boundary tokens ending a segment in structured or boilerplate text, just before a new field or line begins. Typical spots are line breaks between header or diff lines (strongest after an #ifndef include-guard line), the final digit of an ISBN, URL fragment words like 'comments' or 'respond' that precede a timestamp, and punctuation or delimiters in code, URLs and metadata. It fires only rarely on ordinary prose.

15273.name: Definite article "The"/"the" (occasionally other determiners like "These"/"A") at the start of a new sentence, paragraph, or clause, opening a fresh noun phrase that introduces the next topic. Activation is strongest right after a period or paragraph break.

Sentence-initial definite determiners (mostly "The", sometimes "the"/"This") that open a new sentence or clause and begin a noun phrase referring back to something already introduced. Activation is strongest right after a sentence break or paragraph break in news-style prose.

15423.name: Separator and delimiter tokens (spaces, hyphens, periods, slashes) placed immediately before a number or code segment inside structured strings such as DOIs, URLs, dates, file names, version numbers, and metadata like ratings or word/page counts, where a name or word gives way to digits.

Separator tokens, mostly hyphens and bare spaces, that link two alphanumeric segments in URLs, slugs, dates, IDs, product codes and metadata strings. They usually come right before a number, e.g. "Words 3 Pages" or "line 32". A few weak activations fall on ordinary words in prose.

1546.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires across the continuation of an ongoing phrase, clause, or list. It marks the middle and tail tokens that elaborate or complete a structure begun earlier: the remaining list items, argument fields in code, the rest of a purpose or relative clause. It appears in prose, code, citations and dates alike. Activation usually builds toward the end of the unit and stops at sentence or line boundaries, without clear dependence on topic.

A broad, diffuse feature that fires on predictable continuations of text, especially where content repeats or follows an established pattern. It responds most strongly to copying earlier material: repeated phrases, recurring identifiers, lists and sequences (RC17 RC18…, "String #", 666…, "/ / /"), repeated code calls or tags, and formulaic structures like SQL conditions, lambda chains and key-value dicts.

155.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires on content-bearing words across varied text, including code. It is strongest on the head nouns and final subword pieces of specialized or technical noun phrases, especially medical and scientific terms such as 'eye movements', 'saccades', 'syncope' and 'DBS', and on product or entity names. Function words get little activation.

A diffuse, weak feature with no single clear trigger. It fires broadly across structured or technical text (code, markdown tables and lists, math variable definitions, problem statements, garbled or noisy text). Its peaks fall on key content noun phrases or technical terms being specified or defined, such as "throwing exceptions", "Faraday rotation", "tan"/"cot", "MFA" and "Athletes' Association". Secondary activity appears on surrounding formatting tokens like pipes, newlines, brackets and whitespace runs.

15677.name: Main predicates in news-style lead sentences announcing a new event or development, especially the verb phrase right after the subject (e.g. 'has begun production in', 'has launched', 'filed a lawsuit', 'have identified a', 'announced that'). Weaker activation falls on surrounding prepositions, dates and objects in these factual report or headline sentences.

News-style announcement language: the main predicate of a lead sentence reporting a new event or development, typically right after the subject (said/voted/secured/launched/has begun), often with time words (Wednesday, yesterday, this week), 'new', and the clause punctuation that follows. Strongest in press releases and news ledes.

15805.name: Promotional or descriptive text about companies, brands and products. It fires most strongly on brand or company names (Graco, Samsung, ADATA, Philips, Goodrich) and on the words right after them that describe the company, such as "is known for its commitment", "is an awful brand", "from top brands like", "created the" and "Based in… is proud to". It also fires weakly on general marketing or press-release wording.

Mentions of companies, brands, manufacturers and makers (e.g., Patagonia, Nissan, LEGO, Google/Asus, Les Baer Custom, Avid Carp), plus the surrounding text describing what they make, design or do, especially promotional or company self-descriptions ("we produces/designs", "designed by ... built by").

1593.name: A diffuse feature that fires weakly across ordinary prose on function words and parts of fixed multiword phrases, collocations and formulaic constructions (e.g. "is just one of the", "nowhere to be found", "may play a role", "managed to", "seconds away", "did the world a favor"). It peaks on the predictable middle or continuation tokens of these set expressions, typically modifiers, quantifiers, light verbs and prepositions, rather than on content-heavy nouns.

A diffuse, weak feature that fires on ordinary function words and clause-continuation tokens (auxiliaries such as do/does/did/is/are, and words like 'that', 'the', 'in', 'if', 'best', 'final') in the middle of fluent explanatory or instructional prose, especially assistant-style answers, tutorials and code comments. The strongest activations fall on predictable multi-word phrase continuations ('in place at', 'if they are', 'can't seem to stay', 'you want information') rather than on content-specific words.

16079.name: A diffuse, weakly firing feature on discourse pivot points: clause or sentence boundaries (commas, periods, question marks, line breaks) and the words just after them that introduce contrast, debate, criticism or differing viewpoints. Typical triggers are "However, its use has also been criticized", "open to debate", "Experts debate", "some leading experts" and rhetorical questions. It fires most strongly when text shifts toward controversy or evaluation.

Weak, diffuse feature that fires mostly at clause and sentence boundaries, such as periods, paragraph breaks, and the opening words of the next sentence. It is strongest at discourse pivots that introduce a contrast or shift, like "but come up against", "although not without controversy" and "there is debate". It also fires lightly on function words and auxiliaries (has, been, the, ’t) in running prose.

1644.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature that spans ordinary running prose, especially the predicate parts of clauses: verb phrases, their complements, and descriptive or evaluative modifiers ('can present a few extra problems', 'revolve around instant gratification'). Activation rises somewhat in emotionally weighted or reflective statements ('can no longer face the tragedy', 'could signify that'). It largely skips names, numbers and technical labels.

A diffuse, weak feature that fires across running clauses in explanatory, instructional, or assistant-style prose (code comments, math, Q&A, narrative). It tends to activate on function and content words in the middle of elaborating or qualifying phrases (e.g., "not sure about the value", "mind playing tricks", "claimed to have", "very broad from just"), rather than on any specific token type. Activation peaks inside hedging, reasoning, or descriptive continuations.

1648.name: Line-break tokens (newline, often merged with the preceding punctuation such as period, semicolon, brace, colon or quote) that end a line, sentence, heading or code statement, across prose, lists, metadata, LaTeX and code. A single newline tends to activate more strongly than a double newline.

Line-break tokens, often merged with preceding end-of-line punctuation (periods, colons, brackets, backticks, spaces), that end a line of text, code, or a list item. Single newlines fire most strongly, while multiple newlines fire a bit less.

16494.name: Final tokens of the content words in image captions, photo credits and alt-text descriptions, such as places, names, dates and the objects shown. The text often sits just before a line break, a credit like AP or Getty, or the start of an article. Activation is strongest at the end of caption phrases describing location and date, e.g. 'airport in Thailand', 'Festival in France in 2012', 'Oct. 5, 2020'.

Content words in photo-caption-style descriptions of a scene, especially where the event, location (venue, city, country) and date are given (e.g. "speaks at the funeral of… in Tokyo on Saturday"). The strongest activations fall on place names, venue nouns and date tokens in these captions.

1657.name: Content nouns and noun phrases (often multiword compounds or technical/domain terms) that name the key topic entity or concept in a clause, typically the head noun after a preposition or determiner, e.g. object-of-preposition or subject noun phrases. Function words are rarely marked.

Content-word nouns (and noun-modifier compounds) that name the topic, object, or entity being talked about, often the head of a noun phrase after a preposition or determiner (e.g. "the polygon", "chord chart", "team names", "error message"). This shows up across prose, math, and noisy or garbled code and multilingual text, and activation is weak and diffuse.

17181.name: Words for defense (defense/defence, defensive, defender, defending, the D in D-line), strongest in team sports, especially American football and basketball (defensive coordinator, defensive tackle, a team's defense). Weaker for defensive meanings in military, gaming, biology or workplace contexts.

Words built on the root "defen-" (defense/defence, defensive, defending, defender, defensively, defenseman), mainly in sports contexts describing a team's defensive unit, positions, or play. Activation peaks on "defensive" used as a modifier for football positions or team units (defensive lineman/end/back/line/front) and on team defenses, is weaker for soccer "defence," "defending champion," and non-sport or psychological uses.

174.name: A diffuse, weakly firing pattern on content words that complete a phrase, mostly head nouns serving as the object of a verb or preposition (e.g. "raising money", "pet stores", "on walls"). It also fires on some predicate adjectives and participles and on following commas or conjunctions at phrase boundaries. There is no single topic, so it looks like a general marker of a phrase's main noun or argument completion.

Content-bearing words that complete a phrase or clause, mostly the head noun of a noun phrase (often after "the", "a" or a preposition) naming the object of discussion, such as question, code, input, variable, file, help. The text is mostly technical, programming or assistant-style. Weaker activations fall on verbs or participles that end a clause, like done, failed, provided and help.

17413.name: The day number in a written calendar date, usually right after a month name (e.g. "On April 3,"), often with an ordinal suffix like st/th. It fires most strongly in sentence-opening "On [Month] [day]" phrases introducing an event. Where the day comes first ("13 May", "19th November"), the month name is marked instead.
The day-of-month number in a date that follows a month name or numeric month, usually in narrative phrases like "On [Month] [day]" that introduce when an event happened.

17525.name: Software installation and filesystem terms, especially names of directories, folders and file types where programs get installed or stored (e.g. /sbin, /bin, install, binaries, executables, dll, runtime, dev files, scripts, tmp, Applications, program_files). Activation is strongest on path segments and install targets in build or setup instructions. Weak, scattered activations also appear on list punctuation and structural tokens.

Category/type words that classify a resource or component, chiefly in software and computing contexts: directory names in file paths (template, Bin, usr, var, headers, init.d), and modifiers naming a kind of file, code or build element (DLL files, system apps, read-only sections, compile dependency, library path, classpath). It fires more weakly on similar classifier nouns elsewhere (staff, books, assets, parking, stationery).

17543.name: Junctures in procedural or technical text (instructions, API docs, code) where one action or step ends and its result or the next step follows: sentence and clause boundaries after an action, step numbers, "and"/"will" connectives, and especially the hand-off to a response or output (e.g. "Response from the API:", closing parentheses or braces after a call).

Tokens in process or step-by-step descriptions at the point where an action has been performed and its outcome or next stage follows. Typical cues are waiting, a response or feedback, results, success or failure (e.g. 'If your request fails', 'sit back and wait a few minutes', 'a call succeeded') and sentence or step boundaries leading into the next step.

17693.name: Nouns or phrases that name a limit, boundary or capacity that something reaches, runs out of or goes past. These usually follow words like "beyond the", "more than", "greater than the", "end of the", "edge of the", "out of", "exceeds" or "run down the". Typical targets are edge, radius, battery, number of items, maximum allowed, duration and limit; code examples mark the bound variables (lim, $late, payload length).

A limit, capacity, or available amount that something exceeds, drains, or overruns, usually right after words like "exceed", "more than", "greater than", "over the", "off the", "drain the" or "<=". Examples include battery, budget, quota, max, available space, capacity, size of the volume, and .length. Activation is strongest on code bound checks (e.g. ".length" in a length comparison) and on "available" or "capacity of".

17707.name: The verb "issue" in all its forms (issued, issuing, issuance, Japanese 発行), meaning to officially put out or distribute a document, statement, warning, certificate or product. It often extends to the following article (a/an), and fires more weakly on synonyms like "released" or "uttering" and on the look-alike "ISS".

Forms of the verb "issue" (issued, issuing, issuance, issuers), meaning to officially release or distribute something such as statements, warnings, documents, cards, currency, or stamps. A following "a" or "of" is sometimes included. Other tokens show only weak, sporadic activation.

17741.name: Tokens in the middle of a multi-token word, name, or fixed phrase (word fragments like 'un|sc|athed', 'Nan|op|ore', 'Aix|-M|arseille', or function words in set expressions like 'point of view', 'piece of paper', 'all the time', 'up to date', 'U.S.'), where the following token is highly predictable. Activation is often strongest when the phrase repeats earlier text.

Tokens in the middle of a fixed collocation, name, or split word whose continuation is highly predictable: word fragments and first pieces of multi-token words (Obi-W|an, LOS AN|GELES, U|.S., 4 p|.m.), and connecting words in set phrases (more or less, all of a sudden, first of all, exactly the same, shapes and sizes).

17833.name: The first word or two right after an opening article (mostly "The", sometimes "A") at the start of a title, heading or sentence. These are usually the head noun or modifier of a noun phrase, often in a "The X of Y" construction (e.g. Importance, Art, Essence, history).

The first content word (noun or modifier) right after a determiner like "The", "An" or "This", most often at the start of a title, headline or sentence. It marks the head of the opening noun phrase, e.g. "The Power of…", "The film…", "The syndrome…".

18130.name: Unit words that follow a number to state a size, mostly in digital and computing settings. The strongest are "-bit" and "bit" in phrases like 32-bit or 8-bit. Weaker hits include bits, bytes, digit, character, pin, syllable, note, hour and ounces, typically in compound measure phrases such as "N-unit".

Unit or measure words placed directly after a number, typically as compound modifiers like "32-bit", "4-digit", "15-pin", "140 characters", "Gigabit". It is strongest for "bit"/"bits" in computing contexts (bit width, encryption strength) and weaker for digits, pins, ounces, characters and similar units.

1831.name: A diffuse feature firing on content words (mostly nouns, plus some verbs and adjectives) that head a new phrase. These are typically the first meaningful word after a determiner, sentence start or list bullet. The strongest cases are abstract or relational head nouns followed by 'of' (shape of, graph of, effects of, limits of, timing of, interior) and participles opening a clause (Planted, Holding, identified, observed).

A diffuse feature that fires on content words (mostly abstract or generic nouns, plus some verbs and adjectives), typically right after a determiner, preposition or line break. Examples are 'values', 'reception', 'medium', 'concentration' and 'pairs'. It activates sparsely across many tokens in ordinary, and often garbled or spammy, prose. The strongest activations come on nouns that head a noun phrase, such as 'The ___ of' or 'a ___'.

18356.name: Verbs and determiners in calls to submit or send something to someone, such as a comment, message, question, email, or information (e.g. "Leave a", "Send us an email with", "submit questions", "register your"). The phrases often appear in reader-engagement or contact prompts, and the feature fires most strongly on the verb and the following article or possessive, just before the item being sent.

Verbs and following determiners in requests or calls to action asking the reader to provide, send, or contribute something (leave a comment, send photos, email, submit your, bring a, give me your), typically after "please", "you can", or "by".

1857.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires across content-bearing spans in ordinary prose, mainly noun phrases and predicates naming the specific subject, setting or domain of the passage (places, organizations, products, technical or medical terms). Activation peaks on the key topic nouns, such as 'quantum dots', 'Boquete', 'carcinoma' and 'Academic Decathlon', and stays weak on function words and generic connectives.

Diffuse, weak activation over multi-word descriptive noun phrases and their prepositional complements (often following 'the', 'of', 'in'), spanning entity/domain descriptions such as places, organizations, technical items, and groups of people. It peaks on content head nouns and compound modifiers (e.g., 'network security', 'automobile industry', 'stores', 'places'), and on code it fires loosely on identifiers and paths.

1880.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires across many genres (prose, code, technical, legal, recipes) on content-bearing tokens, mainly nouns and noun phrases naming key entities, technical terms, proper names and list items, together with the punctuation or line breaks that close those items. It seems to track salient topic or entity spans rather than any single word or meaning.

A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no sharp semantic focus. It fires on scattered tokens in structured, often synthetic-looking or slightly garbled text such as code, CSS, math and calculations, tables, lists and logic puzzles. It tends to land on key nouns or terms (identifiers, units, named entities like 'root beer', 'MJD', 'container') and on line-ending punctuation or newline/whitespace tokens that close a clause or list item.

18955.name: Word pieces containing "add"/"addle" (often preceded by s), the strongest being "saddle", "sadd" in saddened/saddled, "Saddle River", and "saddle thrombus". Weaker on similar pieces such as straddle, swaddle, paddle, cradle, madden and Saddam, and on other horse-riding or straddling terms (stirrup, astride, bridle).

Word pieces containing the letter sequence "add"/"addle", strongest for "saddle"/"saddled"/"saddening" (also Saddam, Saddleworth, straddle, swaddle, paddle, maddening). Weak activation on similar-sounding fragments like astride, buckle, ashtray.

1902.name: Fires on the first token of a document and, most strongly, on the first break after the opening title or header line: the newline, comma or space that ends a headline, file header or shebang. It also fires on tokens whose next token is nearly certain, such as " don" before 't, "201" or "200" before a year digit, " able" before "to", " such" before "as", "Figure " or "Chapter " before a number, and "utf-" before "8".

A position-based latent with no consistent meaning. It fires moderately on the very first token of a text and peaks on one token shortly afterward, usually within the first several tokens. That peak token is typically a function token such as a period, comma, newline, space or "the", regardless of content or language.

1922.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires at the end of a multi-token term or name, such as the head noun of a compound phrase after a rare or technical modifier ("schedule", "Environment", "framework", "effect", "option") or the final subword of a split word ("ging", "escence"). It also fires on the punctuation, parentheses or newlines that close that phrase. In short, it marks phrase-boundary completion rather than any particular meaning.

A diffuse, low-intensity feature active on garbled, incoherent or degenerate text, such as mixed-language fragments, nonsense pseudo-code, repetitive token loops and broken markup. It fires weakly across many tokens. The strongest activations tend to fall on punctuation, delimiters, colons, closing brackets and line breaks that end a fragment.

1929.name: A weak, diffuse feature spread across ordinary running prose. It shows no single lexical trigger and mostly fires on function words, clause boundaries (commas, periods, "but", "however", "that", "which"), and the content words that continue a clause. It is strongest mid-sentence in expository or narrative text, where the next phrase elaborates, contrasts, or adds a result (e.g., "result in", "contribute to", "downside of").

A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires across long runs of ordinary tokens (function words, nouns, punctuation, code) rather than on any specific word. It is strongest in rambling, semantically incoherent or machine-generated-sounding text, where sentences are grammatical but lose meaning (for example "outcomes befall as a result of human-cetera interaction"). It also appears on garbled code and mixed-language snippets.

19364.name: Tokens marking the start of a new question, problem, or list item, typically after a line break or numbering. These are numerals and their following period or colon, bullets, and the first words of a question or problem statement (e.g., "What/Which/How/Is", "A", "If", "Consider"), common in quiz, homework and Q&A text.

The opening token of a new item, entry, or segment, typically right after a paragraph break, a list/question number ("2.", "Problem 2.", "Q:") or another separator. It fires most strongly at the start of numbered questions, exercises and problems ("A person travels...", "You are shrunk...") and on the numbering itself. The activating words are mostly function words or sentence-starters such as The, A, How, There and I.

1969.name: A diffuse, weakly activating feature on formatting and separator tokens rather than words. It fires mostly on the space before a number ("January 1995", "n = 3"), decimal points and digit chunks inside numbers, DOIs and IDs, and on paragraph breaks or punctuation at section boundaries. The strongest activations are in numeric tables, equations and headings.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires most clearly in numeric contexts. It peaks on the space token before a number (e.g. 'last 26', 'the 762'), on hyphens in scores and vote tallies (53-46, 3-0), and on thousands-separator commas (26,616). It also fires sporadically and weakly on unrelated tokens.

19721.name: Bodily functions and their disorders, chiefly digestion and elimination: bowel, constipation, fiber, bloating, digestive tract, bladder, insomnia, secretion and congestion. Strongest on constipation, fiber and bowel. It also fires weakly on related ideas of flow, blockage or release in non-medical settings, such as clogging drains, stagnant energy and releasing tension.

Words about digestion and bowel function, firing most on constipation and laxatives, then on intestines, bowel habits, digestive disturbances and urination. Weaker activation on other bodily-function or body-care terms involving blockage, release or clearing, such as flossing, exfoliation, clogging, cleansing, cramping and stiffness.

1976.name: Abstract, purpose- or benefit-oriented phrasing typical of mission statements, marketing, and formal expository prose. It is strongest on extended clauses describing goals, capabilities, and outcomes, such as "to help you…", "enabling X to deliver…", "emphasize the importance of…", or lists of verbs like "manage costs, mitigate risks, and maintain…". Activation is spread across whole clauses rather than single words.

A diffuse, low-intensity feature that spans whole stretches of generic, abstract, buzzword-heavy explanatory or corporate prose, such as mission statements, lists of services, benefits, processes and goals (e.g. 'create safer cars', 'protection of… promotion of…', 'Planning, Budgeting, and Project Execution'). It peaks on polished, formulaic phrasing and fires weakly on scattered tokens in incoherent, mixed-language or garbled synthetic text.

19770.name: Restrictive or exclusive focus words, mainly "only" (strongest when "Only" starts a sentence, e.g. "Only those" or "Only now"). They also fire on the determiner or quantifier that follows, such as "only the" or "only a few". Activation is weaker on related limiting or exceptive words like "except", "unless", "not until", "even" and "anything but".

The restrictive/limiting focus word "only" (strongest when it starts a clause, e.g. "Only then" or "only the"), plus the tokens right after it. Weaker hits fall on similar limiting words ("just", "merely", "not every", "even") and on the word following "only" or "just".

19914.name: The word "cell" (also cells/cellular, "Cell" capitalized, or as a fragment like sub-cell-ular) in biological contexts. It is strongest when "cell" acts as a noun modifier in compounds such as cell death, cell division, cell contact, cell cycle and cell viability. Related biological units (neuronal, plant, brain, particle) activate weakly.

The word "cell" (usually singular, lowercase), strongest in biological contexts, especially as a modifier in compounds like cell death, cell growth, cell culture, cell function and cell biology. It fires weakly on "cells", on non-biological senses (cell phone, prison cell, the place name Cellardyke), and on a few other nouns that modify a following noun, such as "plant growth" and "company voluntary".

19927.name: Sentence-ending punctuation fused with line breaks (".⏎⏎", ".⏎", "?⏎⏎") and bare paragraph breaks, firing most strongly at abrupt boundaries in spammy, incoherent or auto-generated web text where the next line begins an unrelated heading, ad or topic.

Sentence- and paragraph-ending boundaries (periods, newlines, especially ".

" and "

") in low-quality, spammy or incoherent web text (SEO/casino/pharma spam, machine-generated gibberish), firing where the text abruptly switches to an unrelated sentence, heading, or boilerplate. Strongest after nonsensical sentences.

Sentence- or line-ending punctuation and newline breaks (especially ".\n\n") that close off a segment in incoherent, spammy or keyword-stuffed web text (SEO spam, casino ads, gibberish), right before an abrupt shift to an unrelated topic or heading. Weaker activations land on other boundary tokens such as runs of spaces, closing brackets, and menu or boilerplate words.

20232.name: Positive aesthetic or admiring adjectives (and related nouns/adverbs) such as "wonderful", "beautiful", "lovely", "delightful", "marvellous" and "beauty". The strongest activations are on "wonderful"/"wonderfully", weaker on "beautiful"/"lovely", and weakest on "beauty" used as a product or category noun.

Positive aesthetic/admiring words, chiefly "wonderful" (strongest), "beautiful", "beauty", and "lovely", plus similar terms like "delightful", "amazing", and "magical", used in any context to praise or describe something pleasing.

2028.name: The preposition "of" (including capitalized "Of" and fused forms like "numberOf"), mostly in noun-phrase constructions that link a head noun to its complement, such as possessive, part-whole, attribute or title relations ("President of", "benefits of", "squares of"). Activation is highest when "of" follows a specific, technical or title-like noun.

The preposition "of" (and its equivalents such as "Of", "-of", or Chinese "的"). It fires most often where "of" links a head noun to its complement ("the Sword of", "a table of", "the odds of"), and also on the "Of" in "Of course".

2044.name: Fires on unnatural, low-quality or garbled text. It is strongest in spun, machine-generated word salad and essay-mill prose, where it covers long runs of incoherent phrasing. It fires weakly on isolated anomalies such as typos, wrong word forms ("critical acclaimed", "filling to", "there me"), odd fragments and artifacts like "[email protected]" or mojibake.

Fires on incoherent, garbled or machine-spun text (word salad, SEO spam, gibberish identifiers), marking tokens that don't fit their context semantically or grammatically. It is strongest on long runs of fluent-sounding but nonsensical prose.

20458.name: Words in decision, approval or voting actions, especially verbs like approved, voted, signed into law, allow or permission and the prepositions or "to" that follow them, right before the object of the decision. Activation peaks on official approval by a governing body ("commission approved to").

Words describing a decision or official action by an authority, board, council, court or voters, especially "approved", along with words like "voted to", "decided to", "consider", "reject", "support", "grants" and the prepositions or articles that introduce the thing being acted on (a measure, budget, plan, project).

20628.name: Function words and punctuation that come right after a topic's subject or title is introduced, usually at the start of a definition or description ("X is a…", "X refers to…", "X has…", a comma or period closing the first descriptive clause). It fires on the verbs, relative pronouns, commas and periods that build an expository opening sentence about a named entity or term, often one just given as a heading.

Function words and punctuation immediately following a just-introduced topic or entity name (usually right after a title or heading), especially the copula/verb that begins its definition or description ("X is a…", "X has…", "X (also known as …) is"). It also fires on the commas and periods that end such introductory, encyclopedic statements.

20653.name: A weak, diffuse feature that mostly fires on discourse connectives and formulaic multi-word phrases that link clauses, such as "on the other hand," "moreover," "however," "then," "in such a way that," "at the time of" and "further I will." It is strongest at the completing word of a fixed expression, for example "hand" in "on the other hand." It appears especially in SEO-style, promotional or non-native web English. It also fires on transliterated Hindi/Urdu words and scattered sentence-ending punctuation.

Markers of Indian/South Asian English: characteristic phrasings and non-native constructions (e.g. 'on basis of', 'keeping in view', 'as per your requirement', 'till date', 'as compared to', 'since…, so', redundant 'then' after 'if', 'etc'). It also fires on South Asian names, terms and contexts (Singh, Jhabak, garam masala, Rs., Sri Lanka, Delhi '011' phone codes).

21011.name: Nouns for a gathered group or assortment of items, chiefly "collection"/"collections", plus related words such as selection, compilation, catalog, archive, library, range, variety, collector, treasure, and curated. Activation is strongest for "collection" itself, especially for museum, library or artist collections and in the phrase "collection of".

Collective nouns for a group of gathered or owned items, chiefly "collection" (strongest, especially a personal or museum collection), plus near-synonyms such as selection, set, line, range, fleet, library, archive, stash and assortment, often followed by "of" plus the items.

21065.name: The determiner (mostly "the") right after a role or affiliation phrase like "director of", "member of", "spokesman for" or "scientist at", introducing the organization, institution or group a person belongs to or leads. It fires most strongly in "head of the" and "co-chair of the" titles.

Determiners (mostly "the", sometimes "a" or possessive "'s") that introduce an organization, institution, group or body after a role or membership phrase, e.g. "president of the", "member of the", "spokesman for the", "head of the". Activation is strongest after leadership or role titles followed by "of".

21199.name: Tokens at the start of, or linking to, a second parallel element that mirrors an earlier phrase with a variation, such as an alternate in parentheses, the second item of a pair or list, a repeated field label, or code lines repeating a prior pattern. The feature anticipates the text echoing a previous structure ("old and my new", "Min… ⏎Volume Range Max", "(maybe Ie7)", "die… open(").

A diffuse feature with no single topic. It fires on function words, connectives (and, to, for, unless, plus) and sentence or line-break punctuation at clause boundaries. It is strongest where the text sets up a parallel, contrastive or repeated structure that echoes earlier wording, such as 'origin and destination', 'not my favorite books', 'carrier sheet', 'compare them to the same edges' and 'second-to-last dimension'.

21458.name: The start of a second predicate in a coordinated clause: the verb, participle or predicative adjective (often with its preposition, e.g. "consists of", "works as", "ranged from") that comes right after "and", "but" or an auxiliary ("and is", "and was") and continues talking about the same subject without restating it.

The verb, or start of the predicate, in a second coordinated clause whose subject is omitted and carried over from earlier, usually right after "and" (sometimes "and is", "but", or "then"). Examples include "and resides on", "and hosted", and "and is teeming".

2162.name: Numbers in running text, whether written as digits or words (cardinal or ordinal), that give a count, quantity, amount, percentage or ranking. The leading number of a phrase activates most, and statistics such as sports tallies activate strongest.

Cardinal numbers (digits or spelled-out words) used as quantities or counts in running text, especially the first number of a phrase. Activation is strongest for sports statistics and tallies such as scores, vote counts, sacks, touchdowns and saves.

21846.name: Tokens that close a unit, typically right after an enumerated list or series of items: final punctuation, closing brackets/quotes/braces, line breaks, or the word right after the list ends. Activation is weak and diffuse, peaking where a list or bracketed/quoted group closes (")", "\"]", " }").

The token right after a list or enumeration of items ends (closing parentheses or brackets, periods, commas, dashes, quotes, newlines, or a connecting word like 'to', 'as', 'and'), marking where the series closes and the main sentence or structure resumes.

2233.name: A weak, diffuse feature with no single trigger word. It fires on the core content of explanatory or defining phrases: the words that say what something is, what it does, or how it works. These phrases typically follow a setup cue such as "i.e.", "that is,", "occurs when", "By that I mean", "governs", "are the", "need to" or "built for". Examples include "an elastic material deforms through a small opening", "how long your armour lasts when" and "do not accommodate naturally the notion of a secret key". Activation is strongest in the middle of such a functional or definitional description, especially on its main noun or verb.

Tokens inside clarifying or definitional phrases that restate or explain what something means or does, typically right after "i.e.,", a colon, an opening parenthesis, or a relative pronoun ("that", "where", "who"). Examples include "relationship is actually linear", "modify the original list" and "how far the object is from the axis". Activation is highest on the core predicate of the explanation, mostly in technical or instructional text.

22433.name: Nouns for external threats or unwanted agents that something defends against, removes or fights off (enemies, invaders, attackers, predators, pests, viruses, disease, asteroids, dust, toxins), usually the object of verbs or prepositions like "against", "combat", "protect from", "remove" or "filter out". It is weaker on other things a system takes in or acts on (food, glucose, sauces, the environment).

Nouns naming the threat, enemy or harmful agent that something defends against, fights, or is protected from (invaders, predators, viruses, foreign substances, enemies, attacks, disease, danger), usually the object of verbs like protect from, stop, fight, kill or intercept. Weak activations appear on unrelated object nouns.

22856.name: Words that name a particular time point when something happens, mainly "day" (also night, year, hour, date, holiday names like Christmas Eve or Thanksgiving), typically in phrases like "the same day", "that day", "launch day" or "the night before" that anchor an event to a specific occasion.

Words naming a specific day or point in time, mostly "day" (strongest in "same day", "first day", "that day", "Christmas day"), plus related time units and occasions such as night, morning, week, year, date, today, and holidays. It also fires on date fragments like ordinal suffixes and day numbers, usually within time-reference phrases such as "on the ___ of".

22878.name: Tokens in academic, scientific, or technical prose that mark scholarly discourse: research and expertise vocabulary (theory, method, study, explanation, foundations, perspectives, expertise), researcher actions (we prove, argue, uncovered, solve this problem), and citation or reference formatting such as titles in quotes, journal abbreviations, and citation counts.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on tokens in technical, academic or methodological contexts, such as text about research, engineering, models, theory, scientific methods and expert explanations. It tends to activate near words like 'models', 'sciences', 'theory', 'engineers', 'research', 'technical' and 'proof and simulation', and on function words inside those passages. It is driven by the expert or scholarly register of the surrounding text rather than by any specific word.

23033.name: Words inside natural-language explanations embedded in technical or code contexts, firing most strongly within code comments (e.g. after //, /*, #, <!--) and descriptive identifiers such as test method names. Activation is weak and diffuse in ordinary prose.

A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no single token trigger. It fires on scattered mid-sentence words, mostly content words and function words inside explanatory or instructional prose. The text is typically technical documentation, code comments, recipes, how-to steps, notes and forms, and the tokens usually fall within phrases describing what something does or what to do.

235.name: Word-initial fragments, usually capitalized or space-prefixed, that begin a longer word split across tokens, such as name parts (Ver, Char, Mel), abbreviations (Rev., prof., Std) and truncated stems (Ex, dist, rep, def, Comp). Activation sits on the first piece, which predicts the rest of the word; full short words like obj, err and Pro also fire.

Word-initial fragment tokens: the first subword piece of a longer word that is split across multiple tokens (e.g. "param"-etric, "Rec"-all, "Lib"-elle, "Met"-roid, "dir"). They also include truncated identifiers and abbreviations in code (len, int, del, _prod). The feature seems to mark an incomplete word stem that predicts a continuation, and it shows up most in noisy, technical, or garbled text.

23582.name: Words that introduce the result or product of a transformation, conversion, reaction or formation: prepositions and verbs such as "into", "to", "to form", "produce", "yielding" and "create" placed right before the resulting substance or form (e.g., "converting X into", "react to form", "reduced to"). Activation is strongest for chemical and physical reaction contexts like "react to form" and "decays to form". Weaker activation falls on list conjunctions joining multiple products.

Words marking the result or output of a transformation, conversion or production process. Most often "into" after verbs like turn, convert, transform or change, but also "to", "as", "produce", "generate", "release" and "get". The word links a source to what it becomes or yields.

23762.name: Place names, mostly cities, towns and neighborhoods. Activation falls on the token that completes the name, often a suffix fragment such as "ington", "ville", "ley" or "burg", or the second word of a multiword name like Santa Barbara or Orland Park. These names usually appear in addresses, datelines or institutional affiliations.

Place names, mostly cities and towns (often US college or mid-sized towns), with activation landing on the token that completes the name, such as the final subword or the second word of a multi-word name (e.g. "ston" in Evanston, "Haven" in New Haven). Activation is strongest in locative contexts like "in X" or "based in X". It occasionally also fires on venue names, university domains and person names.

23827.name: Administrative boilerplate covering access, permissions, contact details and usage terms: tokens in instructions about whom to contact, how to obtain or use material (accounts, licenses, membership, availability, restrictions), and disclaimers or correspondence notes. Activation is strongest on directive phrases like "are required to contact" or "are urged to consult".

Words in formal boilerplate or notice-style text about access, availability, permission, restrictions and contact procedures (e.g. 'available from', 'contact … by writing to', 'requires a special permit', 'may not be copied', 'with permission'). They are mostly function words and predicates that link a resource to how, where or under what conditions it can be obtained or used.

24029.name: The comma (or semicolon) right after a surname in inverted "Surname, Given-name" form, as in author lists, citations and bibliographies. It also fires weakly on other separators after a leading name or term ("Place, Region", "Term, qualifier").

Commas placed right after a surname (often an unusual or foreign one) in "Lastname, Firstname" inverted order, as in author lists, citations, bibliographies and obituaries. Sometimes the following initial or first-name token fires instead, and weakly the comma after a place name or other proper noun.

245.name: Weak, diffuse feature on the token immediately following a number or completed noun phrase, usually a connector or separator leading to the next item: range and comparison words ("to", "and", "than", "more"), math operators (+, =, ×, )/( ), dashes, spaces, commas, newlines, and units. It is most common right after numeric values in ranges, equations, dates and measurements.

Separator or connector tokens that come right after a number (or a numeric or other item) and link it to a following value. Typical cases are hyphens, dashes, slashes, plus signs, ±, commas and line breaks in scores, records, ranges, page spans and table cells, e.g. 3-0, 15 - 10, 9st 4lb / 130lb. Weaker activations fall on short words that play the same linking role after an item (in, and, at, than, for).

24738.name: The "pom" letter sequence across words and languages: whole tokens like "pomp" (pompous), "Pom" (Pomodoro, Pompidou, pom-pom) and Czech/Slavic "pom" (pomalu, pomáhají), plus "om/ome/omer/um" pieces right after a split-off "P/p" (Pompeo, pomegranate, Pomeranz, pummeled). Activation is strongest on "Pom"/"pom" tokens.

Word-piece tokens for the sound "pom"/"om" (and similar "um"/"omm"), mostly right after a "P" (or L/G) at the start of a word. Activation is strongest for a capitalized " Pom" opening a proper noun (Pomona, Pomsky, Pompidou, Pomodoro, Pomc) and for "Pompe"/"pomp", and weaker for mid-word fragments like p-ome-granate, p-um-meled, L-om-ax and G-om-el.

24747.name: The subword token "uz" (and close variants such as "Suz", "Luz", "uzz", "z"), mostly found inside proper names and foreign words like surnames, place names and brands (Suzuki, Soyuz, Fuzhou, Kreuz-). Activation is strongest when it falls mid-word in an unfamiliar name.

The subword "uz" (and close variants like " Luz", " Suz", "uzz", "z", "Z", "ž", Cyrillic "з") appearing inside words, mostly proper nouns such as surnames, given names and place names (e.g. Kuznets, Guzman, Luzon, Suzie), plus slang spellings like "cuz"/"duz".

24849.name: Job titles and occupational roles, especially the head noun completing a position name after a modifier (e.g., editorial assistant, acquisitions officer, security guard, Audit Senior, DevOps expert), plus occasional work-related nouns or activities.

Job titles, occupations and professional roles, with activation on the head noun or final subword that completes the role (e.g. clerk, driver, designer, attorney, gunner). It also fires weakly on related work or field nouns (management, design, instruction). Activation is strongest in job-posting or hiring contexts.

25173.name: Words for entry points and ways in or through: entrance, entry, gate, door, access, portal, gateway, intake, ingress, mostly physical but also figurative. Activation peaks on "entrance", especially "the entrance (of/to)", and the following "of" or "to" also fires.

Words for entry and threshold points of a place, such as entrance, entry, gate, gateway, door, lobby, foyer, exit, front and access, plus verbs like enter. It is strongest on "entrance", especially "entrance to/of" a physical place like a mine, tunnel, station or restaurant.

25214.name: Initial tokens of proper names, chiefly Scottish/Irish "Mc" surnames and brands (strongest on "McDonald", especially the restaurant chain; also McKinsey, McLaren, McCormick). Weaker hits on other name-start pieces like "Maurit" (Mauritius/Mauritania), Kellogg, Tiffany and Suzuki, and on fast-food words.

Strongest on the name "McDonald", especially the fast-food chain McDonald's, and weaker on other "Mc"/"Mac" surnames (McConnell, McKinsey, McGuire). It also fires on related fast-food words ("fast food", Happy Meal, burger) and on brand or place names that look like surnames (Tiffany, Kellogg, Buckingham, Coventry).

25249.name: Nouns for retail establishments, mainly "store"/"stores", plus "shop(s)", "retailer", "bookstore", "supermarket" and Chinese 店. They often follow a modifier naming what is sold (grocery, toy, comic book) or a brand name (Honeywell Store). Activation is strongest for "store", weaker for "shop", and also fires on the idiom "in store".

Nouns for retail establishments, mainly "store" and "shop" (plus plurals and compounds like bookstore, storefront, boutiques, in-store). They cover physical and online stores (App Store, iTunes store), and occasionally storage senses such as evidence stores, ammunition store, or the code term Store/load. Activation is strongest for "store"/"stores" in the retail sense and weaker for "shop".

254.name: Fires on non-English text (Danish, Dutch, Russian, Greek, Bengali, Japanese, Azerbaijani, Spanish, French, German), mostly on word-continuation subword pieces, inflectional endings and short function words, and most strongly in longer foreign-language passages.
