It also fires on words tied to the other senses of 'product' and to bilateral exchange, such as 'Products', 'trade', 'free trade', 'Commerce', 'partnership', 'alliances' and 'business partners'. The strongest activations come from mathematical product contexts.

50969.name: The word "behavior/behaviour" (and "behave/behaves/behaved") plus related terms for how something acts, operates, or responds (functionality, functioning, act strangely/differently, what happens, behave this way/fashion). It fires most strongly on the noun "behavior" when it refers to how a system, program, object, or phenomenon operates.

Words for how something acts or functions, chiefly "behavior/behaviour" and its verb forms (behave, behaves, behaving), plus near-synonyms like act, performance, treatment, response and fashion. Activation is highest for the noun "behavior" used in technical or analytical contexts, such as software behavior, the exact behaviour, qualitative behavior, or the behavior of a system.

51143.name: The word "being" and closely related welfare terms: strongest on "-being" completing "well-being" (and "wellbeing"/"wellness"). It fires more weakly on "being(s)" as a noun for an entity or existence ("human beings", "living beings", "state of being") and on "welfare".

The word "being" used as a noun, peaking in "well-being"/"wellbeing" (health, welfare sense). It also fires more weakly on "being(s)" meaning an entity or existence (human beings, magical beings, one's being) and on related welfare words like "wellness" and "welfare".

51232.name: Citation and reference markers in academic or encyclopedic prose: the opening bracket/parenthesis and the digits of reference numbers (e.g. [13], (2), .[19]) and of author–year citations (e.g. (Mark, 1985; ...)), firing most strongly on the final year digit. It also fires weakly at points where a statement ends and a source or attribution follows, such as punctuation before a speaker's name or words like "previously" and "below".

Citation and attribution markers right after a claim or statement: academic references (opening parentheses, author-year dates, et al., bracketed footnote numbers like [5] or .[3]), plus similar source cues such as "according to", "he said", closing quote-comma before a speaker, and URL fragments. The year digit or footnote number activates most strongly.

51302.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires mostly on tokens that complete a phrase or clause, typically the head noun ending a noun phrase (e.g., platform, market, rotor, happiness), and on the punctuation that follows, such as periods, commas or newlines. Occasionally it spreads across short continuation spans right after a sentence boundary (e.g., "The chart suggests", "The benefits ... from CBD is greatly affected"), suggesting a general clause-boundary or phrase-closure signal.

A diffuse, weakly selective feature with no clear lexical target. It fires at low levels on scattered function words, sentence-ending punctuation (often a period before a line break), and occasional content nouns in ordinary running prose. Its strongest activations come as long contiguous spans across whole clauses in conversational, instructional or promotional sentences, for example 'colors for your convenience... are saved', 'conclude that if they can't finish it on normal mode' and 'is to be the leading trusted online source'.

51492.name: Text inside error, warning or status messages from software and systems (e.g. "No address found", "failed to destroy network for", "Access Denied", "Operation timed out", "Prototype mismatch"), especially quoted or logged failure strings. The strongest activations fall on the failure words themselves (found, failed, denied, mismatch). Many weak activations are scattered over unrelated technical or code tokens.

Text of error, warning and system status messages: words inside quoted or reported software errors and failure notices (e.g. "invalid input syntax", "could not connect", "no longer supported", "unable to save", "cannot be empty", "not found"). The strongest responses are on negations and failure terms ("not", "invalid", "error", "No"). There are weaker hits on boilerplate website notices ("you're using an unsupported browser", "you already have an account") and scattered technical tokens.

51568.name: The word "affair(s)" (incl. French "affaire", "Public/Home Affairs", "state of affairs", love affair, all-day affair) is the strongest trigger. Weaker hits go to near-synonyms for general domains or concerns after a modifier, such as matters, issues, business, relations and things.

The word "affair(s)" in all its senses: a domain or field (public, foreign, rural, world, current affairs, often in department or job titles), an event or occasion ("an all-European affair", "a messy affair"), and a romantic affair. It fires most strongly on "affairs"/"Affairs". Near-synonyms for a subject or business, such as matters, relations, liaison, business and fiasco, fire weakly.

51644.name: Internet laughter or reaction slang in casual writing, mainly "lol"/"LOL", along with "haha", "kek", "OMG" and emoticons. It fires most strongly on a standalone "lol" placed at the end of a clause or sentence. It also fires weakly on look-alike letter strings such as "Lol" in "Lollipop", "Lolwe", "Lollapalooza" and "LOL" as in League of Legends.

Internet slang laughter/reaction interjections in informal text, chiefly "lol"/"LOL" (strongest), plus variants like "lulz", "LMAO", "haha", "hehe", and weaker "OMG"; often the final token completing the acronym, typically placed at the end of a sentence or clause.

51915.name: The first token of a direct object or argument: a determiner, opening quote or parenthesis, or the first piece of a multi-token name or identifier. It typically follows a verb, preposition, or function call (e.g. print(lst, open TEST, into conf, the + noun). Activation is weak and diffuse, and is somewhat stronger for code identifiers and function arguments.

Tokens that open a noun phrase or multi-part name/identifier right after a verb or preposition, where the following token completes a specific entity. These include determiners after instruction verbs in recipes ('add the', 'whisk together the', 'cutting your'), first subword fragments of names or codes ('Ch|aitanya', 'R|ijiju', 'K|ARB', 'i|Red', 'Sim|Cash'), hyphens inside alphanumeric labels ('RM-131', 'carbon-13') and labels like 'Step'/'Group' that precede an index.

5200.name: Whitespace tokens (often unusual or non-breaking spaces) immediately preceding a special Unicode symbol such as an emoji, ℃, ω, ⌚ or ‹. More weakly, the feature fires on stray formatting and encoding artifacts like Â, €, BOM or directional marks, combining diacritics in kaomoji, bullets (•, ·, ●) and list-number punctuation.

Weak, diffuse activation on unusual or non-standard characters and encoding artifacts: special Unicode symbols (bullets, emoji, zero-width/invisible spaces, BOM, variation selectors, braille blank), odd whitespace before non-Latin text, mojibake fragments, HTML entities, and escaped unicode sequences.

52443.name: Words and word pieces expressing permanence, endlessness or long duration (eternal, enduring, perpetual, lasting, perennial, timeless, immortal, endless, infinite, lifelong). "Eternal" fires most strongly, and related mortality and age terms fire weakly.

Words expressing permanence, endless duration or timelessness (eternal, timeless, forever, enduring, lasting, lifelong, posterity, immortal, endless, infinite). Activation is strongest for "eternal" and "timeless", and weaker for related ideas of longevity, great age, or transience (ephemeral).

52686.name: A weak, diffuse feature. It mostly fires at clause and sentence boundaries (commas, periods, newlines, a following "The/He/I") that come right after scene-setting phrases naming an event, place or time, such as "at a funeral,", "conference, in New York.", "this week," and "on my aunt's wedding day,". It also fires on words that lead into what happened or what was observed: see, find, what they hear, had, was. Overall it marks the transition from framing context into the narrated content.

A diffuse feature in news-style or narrative prose, firing weakly on sentence boundaries (periods, paragraph breaks) and the subject/auxiliary/main verb that opens the next clause ("was attended", "will be looking for", "were told", "is"). It often appears right after an event, meeting, conference or person has been introduced, where the text moves on to report what happened or how people reacted.

52837.name: Pronoun subjects (it, I, we, they, you, she, he, there) and the auxiliary or copular verbs right after them ('s, 're, was, is, can, will be) that begin a new clause. Activation is strongest on contractions like "it's" and "I'm" in conversational or quoted speech.

Sentence-initial subject pronouns (it, they, we, you, he) and the auxiliary/copular verbs or contractions right after them ('s, are, have, was, 're), mostly in quoted, conversational speech. The activation is on the subject and verb that open a new clause, often at the start of a new sentence inside a quote.

52965.name: Forms of the verb "consist" (consist, consists, consisted, consisting, and the split piece "ist"), almost always directly followed by "of" or "in" to introduce the components or content of something.
Forms of the verb "consist" (consists, consisting, consisted, consist), typically followed by "of", that introduce what something is made up of or contains.

53002.name: Coordinating or linking words (mostly "and", also "or", "but", "with", "along with", "coupled with", "alongside other", "and other") that come right after a completed noun phrase or clause, often one ending in a demonstrative like "this/these/that/it". They mark the start of a second item or action joined to the first.

Coordinating conjunctions and connectors (mostly "and", also "or", "but also", "with") right after a completed noun phrase or clause, where they extend it with another item or action. Activation is strongest for additive phrases like "and other reasons", "and many others" and "or any", which add further entities to an established subject.

53164.name: Tokens forming identifiers, field or column names, keys, and labels in structured data or technical text, such as database columns, JSON or array keys, variable or property names, form or UI labels, and named components. Activation is strongest on schema-like field names in code, for example SQL column definitions like ad_id and source.

Tokens forming the key word of a label, field, or attribute name, often completing a compound identifier or name: data/schema keys and column names (published_at, file_stage, _status, .name, -size, ArticleType, HOST), form/metadata labels (Author, Description, Type, Company, job title, publisher), and the head word of compound named items (Rotten Egg, Charcoal, Sigil Stone, Court St, Floor Assembly). Activation is strongest in code and structured-data contexts.

53399.name: Fractional or secondary parts of compound quantities: the token that adds a fraction or sub-unit to a whole number, such as "half" in "an hour and a half", the digit after a decimal point (2.5), "⅓" or "1/4", and smaller units following a larger one ("5 feet 8 inches", "18 months"). The strongest signal is on "half"/"-half" and fraction symbols.

Fractional or secondary parts of a numeric quantity: digits after a decimal point, the "/2" of mixed fractions like "1 1/2", "half" in "X and a half", and smaller units following a larger one (e.g., "3 years 4 months", "12 feet, 2 inches"). Strongest on "half" and "1/2" completing compound quantities.

53724.name: Words that open or carry a question or inquiry: interrogatives (what, why, how, who, which, whether, if), question-starting auxiliaries (Does, Can, Is), and the words right after them inside direct or embedded questions. It also fires on title or headline phrases that set up a topic to be explained, such as 'explore how', 'types of', 'common myths', 'Secret To' and 'Promo Codes'. Activation is highest at the start of a question clause.

Tokens inside questions or indirect questions, most strongly in the words that open them or carry them along (wh-words, auxiliaries/modals like 'could', 'would', 'can you', 'is it possible'). Activation is highest on direct questions and query phrasing ('How did this happen?', 'what price tag would I be looking at', 'Can you tell me how to'). It is weaker on embedded clauses of uncertainty ('find out who', 'know what to get') and on content that is speculative or inquisitive.

53801.name: Numeric expressions and their surrounding tokens: leading spaces before numbers, first digit chunks (e.g. "200", "199" in years), and internal separators (commas, periods, hyphens, colons) within quantities, dates, ranges, prices, phone numbers and addresses. It is strongest on counts and ranges preceded by words like "over", "than" or "in" ("over 22,000", "3-4 weeks", "$1").

Tokens right before an upcoming number, mostly the lone space token (or a leading digit chunk, "$", "#", separators like ",", "-", "/"). It fires where a numeral is predicted next, as in years, counts, quantities, ranges, dates, times and addresses, often after words like "in", "since", "than", "between", "within", "and".

54199.name: Numbers used as reference locators in citations, mostly page numbers and page ranges (especially the end of a range), but also verse, line, volume, case-reporter and diff line numbers, plus timestamp minutes. A few weak hits on unrelated tokens like "and" or line breaks.

Numbers that serve as locators inside references, chiefly page numbers in citations (e.g. "p. 199", "Id. at 733", a pinpoint page after a case reporter volume and first page). Activation is strongest for legal case pin cites like "18 Or 126, 138". It also fires weakly on the final digits of timestamps (minutes) and the trailing digits of document or post IDs.

54286.name: Tokens marking the end of a clause, sentence, list item or code statement: final words completing a phrase (e.g. 'Shop Now', 'new growth', 'login') and boundary tokens such as periods, commas, semicolons, closing parens and newlines. Activation is strongest at code statement endings and function calls like '$apply()' and ');'.

Fires at the end of clauses describing a procedural step, especially one that restores, repeats, or keeps a prior state (refresh/reload the page, re-pair, refill, repower, retry, repeat, return, again, maintain the existing profile). Activation usually lands on the final token or punctuation (period, comma, newline, 'and') that closes the step before the next one begins.

544.name: Tokens inside or just entering literal, formatted, or quoted content: code lines, shell and SQL commands, config options, preprocessor directives, formulas, rule specifications, and delimiters (colons, newlines, quote marks, bullets) that set off such content. Activation is strongest within command or code snippets that follow an introductory colon or newline.

A diffuse, mostly weak feature that fires at boundaries where literal text is about to be entered or quoted. It is strongest on command or code strings the reader is told to type or add, such as 'net user administrator /active:', 'Add "blacklist', 'PRINT(' and mailcap file entries. It fires more weakly on the colons, quote marks and line breaks that introduce such strings, and on verbs like type, call and search.

545.name: Words and phrases that express variety, variation, diversity or dependence on circumstances, such as "various", "different", "wide range of", "depends on", "range from", "customizable", "tailored to your needs", "varying degrees" and "from country to country". The strongest activations fall on the core words signaling multiplicity or variability.

Words and phrases expressing variability, diversity, or dependence on conditions: e.g. "varies based on", "depending upon", "different ways/materials", "various reasons/sizes", "a variety of", "regardless of", "dependent on", "ranging". Activation peaks on verbs like "varies" and on nouns marking multiple options or kinds.

5476.name: Mostly whitespace runs (multiple spaces, single spaces before bullets or values) used for alignment/padding in code, config files, tables and lists; strongest on long space runs between columns or fields. Weak secondary firing on punctuation/newline separators and filler tokens.

A diffuse feature that fires on tokens inside formulaic, highly predictable text, typically mid-phrase where the next token is near-certain. Contexts include newsletter, cookie and signup boilerplate ("Sign up to receive", "like to send you offers and news"), hard line breaks that split common phrases ("According⏎to", "During⏎the"), and line counts in diff hunk headers. It also responds to stretched or repeated characters ("oooooooo", "mm", "))))", dot leaders), and to spacing or field tokens in structured listings such as "$ 6", "Size/Form" and "Join Date".

5553.name: Location-related words, mainly "where" (and somewhere/anywhere/wherever), plus the clause that follows them, such as "where the physician holds their" or "Where are they". Activation is strongest on "Where" opening direct or indirect questions about a place ("Where can I", "where to go with"). It is weaker on locative relative clauses and on other wh-question phrases.

The word "where" (and variants like Where, wherever, anywhere, somewhere) introducing a location clause or question, plus the clause words right after it (subject, verb, e.g. "where it was coming", "where my mom got"). It is strongest for "where" questions and indirect questions, and weak on related location or question words (places, when, how).

55676.name: The word "current"/"currently" (and Current in identifiers like GetCurrent), meaning present or active state, especially in technical contexts (current location, time, buffer, session, directory). Weaker on other present-time words (now, today, right now) and look-alike tokens such as "content".

The word "current" (and "currently") used to mean the present or active instance of something. Activation is strongest in technical and software contexts such as the current document, file, domain, hour, speed or the currently playing station. Weaker activations come from related words like "present", "selected", "now" and "next", and from "Current" used as a name.

55748.name: Text that states what a system, device, or program displays, reports, or claims, such as error messages, status indicators, and warnings (e.g. "the password is incorrect", "invalid argument", "USB devices not recognized", "the folder is empty"). These usually come right after verbs like says, shows, is telling, or indicates, and are mostly found in tech troubleshooting text.

Text describing technical problems, chiefly error messages, system warnings and status notices from software or devices (e.g. 'unable to save display settings', 'invalid package file', CRYPTO_LIBRARY_INTERNAL_ERROR, 'marked as dirty'). Activation is highest on the quoted or named error and status text, and weaker on nearby troubleshooting terms such as loading, connection, update and powering issues.

55797.name: Head nouns (often abstract or generic) that complete a noun phrase, typically after a determiner or modifier ("the", adjective, compound modifier) and often followed by "of", a preposition or punctuation. The feature fires on the main noun of a phrase rather than on any particular topic.

Generic common nouns that head a noun phrase, usually right after a determiner or preposition ("the", "a", "its", "an"). They name an entity whose specific identity comes from the surrounding context (the case, the deal, the crisis, an office, the program), and they are often followed by a period, comma or prepositional phrase.

56007.name: The word "parking" (and related "parked"/"park"/"car park"), especially as a modifier before lot, garage, space, or area. Weaker activation on related vehicle and storage terms like car, vehicles, seat, and moored.

The word "parking" (and related forms like "Parking", "parked", car "park"), especially in "parking lot" and amenity listings (free/on-site parking). Weaker activation on related vehicle-storage terms (garage, car, moorage, lane, charging).

56801.name: Terms for natural selection and related evolutionary or shaping forces, strongest on "selection" and "selecting for", also firing on fitness, selective force, adaptation, competition, reinforcement and similar mechanism and pressure words that favor or filter outcomes.

Terms tied to Darwinian evolution, chiefly the word "selection" in natural/sexual/artificial selection or "under selection", which fires strongest. Weaker hits include evolutionary pressure, survival of the fittest, fitness, Darwin, eugenics and intelligent design. Non-biological uses of "selection" or "pressure" (self-selection, team selection, selling pressure) fire weakly.

569.name: Content words and connectives inside formal, expository explanation, mostly in scientific, technical, business or educational prose. Activation is strongest on long stretches of explanatory clauses that state causes, requirements, consequences or mechanisms, such as 'leading to', 'due to the presence of', 'may be' and 'require'. Isolated words in casual or listing text activate only weakly.

Weak, diffuse activation across formal expository prose, such as academic abstracts, technical descriptions and SEO or marketing copy. It fires on mid-sentence spans of abstract, jargon-heavy phrasing: nominalizations ("use of…metabolism", "perception of quality of life", "diversity of ordered architectures"), connective prepositions and conjunctions (of, to, and, over), and purpose clauses ("to obtain", "to seamlessly integrate"). Activation is strongest inside long, formulaic descriptions of processes, relationships or goals, and is not tied to any specific word.

57328.name: Sports-venue and location terms about where a game is played, chiefly "home" and "road" (home game, road favorites, at home, on the road), along with "away", "visitors/visiting", "host" and stadium or city names. Weaker activations come from other sports and betting jargon such as derby, serve, blind, spread and bye.

Words marking where a sporting event takes place relative to the teams, i.e. home vs. away. The strongest activations are on "home", "away" and "road (trip)" in game contexts. Weaker activations fall on related venue and travel terms: at, travel to, visited, venue, host, hometown, neutral field, crowd, stadium.

5743.name: Tokens marking the end of a line, item, heading, or clause, usually a newline or terminal punctuation fused with a newline (".⏎", "?⏎", ":⏎"). They appear after list items, titles, questions, code comments, and table cells, at boundaries where one unit ends and the next begins. Activation is strongest at newlines closing code comments or declarations.

Tokens that close off a sentence, line, list item, heading or table cell: final punctuation fused with newlines (".⏎", ".⏎⏎", "?⏎⏎"), bare newlines after list items or code comments, and closing HTML tags ("</") that end cell or heading content. Activation is strongest where the end of one unit leads into another parallel item, such as numbered steps, bullets, enum variants or table cells.

Line-ending and segment-ending tokens (newlines, often fused with a period, question mark, colon or comma) that close a short self-contained unit such as a list item, heading, code comment, title or question, right before a new item, line or section starts. Activation is strongest after code comments and at line breaks within structured or list-like text.

57515.name: Separator tokens (newlines, commas, periods/semicolons plus newline, closing quote/paren) that end one item in a list or enumeration and come right before the next item, especially bulleted or numbered lists. Activation is highest at separators in the middle of a list, where more items clearly follow.

Separators that end one item in a list or sequence of parallel entries, usually the newline (often with trailing punctuation like . ? ” ) >) that follows a list item, bullet, step, ingredient or domain name. It is strongest in long repetitive lists. Commas, semicolons or periods that separate items in inline enumerations activate it more weakly.

57668.name: Paragraph/section break tokens (double newlines, often fused with a final period or other punctuation) that end a sentence, list, or block and come right before a new paragraph, heading or topic shift. Activation is strongest at section boundaries where the following text starts a new unit.
Paragraph-break tokens (double newline, often fused with a period or closing quote/punctuation) that end one text segment and precede a new section, often an abrupt topic or format shift.

5802.name: Words about strictness, rigidity and tightness versus their opposite, looseness or flexibility: strict, rigid, rigorous, tight, stiff, formal, restrictions, enforced, repression, discipline, flexible, tension. It extends to related senses of severity, constraint and exactness, such as technically, proper and abruptly. "Strictly" activates most strongly, followed by rigid, tight and rigorous.

Words about strictness, rigidity, and how tight or loose something is, in both a physical and a rule-based sense. The strongest hits are strict/stricter, stringent, tight/tighten and stiff. Weaker hits are related ideas such as enforcement, restrictions, formal, mandatory, harsh, uncompromising and meticulous, along with their opposites: loose, flexible, lenient and relaxation.

58135.name: Sentence boundaries where the period and the start of the next sentence are merged into one token because the space after the period is missing (e.g. ".The", ".In", ".A", ".B"). These fire most strongly. Weaker hits are other malformed boundaries: a missing period before the next sentence, merged punctuation like ".," or "..", stray spaces, and quote-plus-word tokens at a sentence start.

The start of a new sentence that directly follows the previous sentence's punctuation with no space, so the token fuses the period (or comma, quote, ellipsis) with the first letters or word of the next sentence (e.g. ".The", ".W"). Activation is strongest for these fused period+capital tokens and weaker for ordinary sentence-initial words after spaces, newlines or quotes.

58233.name: Syntax and delimiter tokens inside code, shell commands, markup and URLs, such as quote marks closing attribute values, opening angle brackets, command-line flag dashes, commas between arguments, colons, slashes, query separators (?, &) and opening parens or quotes. Prose tokens appear only weakly.

Weak, diffuse activations spread across many contexts. The clearest pattern is tokens that open or introduce a literal argument or specification, especially in code, shell commands and markup. Strongest are command-line flags ("-o", "-g", "-c") and tag/markup delimiters ("</", "<", "\", "{", quotes). Other examples are separators before a parameter or value (":", "=", "\",\n"). In prose, it fires faintly on words that introduce a means or condition, such as "using", "with", "by" and "set to".

58251.name: The word "lineup"/"line-up" and related ideas of arranging things in a row or a set of members (lineup, roster, matchup, formation, batting order). It also fires on the particle "up" after line/match/measure, as in "lined up" or "match up". Activation is strongest for "lineup" meaning a band's members, product range, team or roster.

The "up" in "line up"/"lineup" and similar phrasal-verb particles (lined up, stack up, match up, pair up), strongest on the noun "lineup"/"line-up" meaning an arranged set of performers, players, or products (roster, product lines, matchups).

The "up" particle in arrangement/alignment compounds and phrasal verbs, especially "lineup"/"line up" and also "matchup", "stack up", "shape up" and "next up". Activation is strongest on the noun "lineup" meaning a set of band members, products or shows, with the related word "roster" also firing. The common sense is arranging items or people in order or pairing them for comparison.

58277.name: The name "Dennis" and its variants (Denis, Denise, Denn-), firing on the name token or its suffix piece ("ennis", "is", "ise") after a split "D"/"Den". "Dennis" activates most strongly, while Denis and Denise (including place names like Saint-Denis and "Denisovans") activate moderately. Unrelated tokens show only faint activation.

The name "Dennis" (strongest), plus related or similar-sounding forms such as Denis, Denise, and Denny, including name fragments after "D"/"Den" ("enny", "ise"). Weaker activation appears on lookalike subwords like "ennis" in "Tennis" and "ener" in "Tenerife".

5840.name: Tokens right at the start of a document, usually the second or third token of an opening title, headline or first sentence. Often this is the word-completion piece after a split first word (e.g. "Ins|pection", "E|levated") or the word right after a first word like "How", "The" or "We". Activation is strongest near the very beginning and fades soon after.

Fires on the first few tokens at the very start of a document (titles, opening sentences, code headers), typically the token(s) right after the first token, often completing a split first word or continuing the opening phrase; position-based beginning-of-text detector rather than content-specific.

Tokens near the very beginning of a document, usually the second token or the next few that complete the first word or phrase of a title or heading (e.g. the rest of a split first word, or the word right after an opening word like "#include", "A", "#").

5847.name: Final tokens of proper names and named entities, especially institutions, organizations, publications and place names (e.g. 'Institute in Boulder, Colo', 'University College London', 'Vanity Fair', 'Protection Agency'). Activation is strongest on the closing word of multi-word names and on location tags after affiliations, and also fires on name-completing subword pieces and unit or technical terms.

Tokens within specific factual details in news-style text, mostly the later parts of proper nouns and named entities (places, organizations, people, teams, products) such as name suffixes, city/state pairs, street addresses, and institution words like Center, University, Council, Corp. It also covers concrete specifics like dates, days, times, numbers and job titles.

58591.name: The word "opposition" and related terms for groups or stances against an established power, such as the political opposition, minority party, challengers, dissidents, rebels, resistance and civil society. Activation is highest for the political sense (opposition parties versus a ruling government) and weaker for the general sense of being "in opposition to" something.

The word "opposition" and related nouns for opposing or rival groups. It fires most strongly on political opposition parties, leaders and groups, more weakly on opposition as resistance to a policy. Related words such as opponents, rivals, rebel, Minority (as in Senate or House Minority Leader), dissent and factions also activate it.

5879.name: Conditional clauses. Fires most on the word "if" (also "if possible", "see if", code `if(`) that starts a condition, and weakly on the subject/verb tokens inside an already-opened "If …" clause (e.g., "If the body…", "If your router has a…").

Weak, diffuse feature centered on words that introduce conditions, constraints or qualifications, mainly "if" (often sentence-initial), "unless", "as long as", "whether", "nor", and modal or limiting words such as "may", "must not" and "only". These appear in rule-like or instructional statements. It also fires on scattered function words inside such conditional or contrastive clauses.

58915.name: Continuation subword pieces that finish rare or multi-token words, mostly proper nouns such as personal names, places, brands, products, teams and mythological or historical names. Examples include Maxim-us, Ab-el-ton, Carth-aget, H-okusai and Na-utilus. It occasionally fires on a whole word that ends a name or title (e.g. Falls, Button, Shepard). Activations are weak overall.

Final tokens of proper names (brands, places, groups, titles, people), especially the subword pieces that finish an uncommon multi-token name like Cerber-us, Koy-ote or Mor-pheus. Activation peaks at the point where the name is completed.

59350.name: Names of government tax and revenue authorities, mainly the IRS, "Revenue" in Internal Revenue Service and Canada Revenue Agency, and HMRC, plus weaker hits on other tax terms, tax laws, and federal or regulatory agencies such as the ATF, DMV, SSA and Treasury.

Names of tax authorities and related government revenue/regulatory agencies, chiefly the IRS ("Internal Revenue Service", "IRS", "irs"), with similar but weaker activation on other tax bodies (HMRC, ATO, Department of Revenue, Customs and Excise) and other federal agency names (ATF, USCIS, BMV). It also fires weakly on tax-related terms like taxman, tax code/rules/policy, audit and CPA. Activation is strongest on the distinctive word or acronym within the agency name, especially "Revenue".

59830.name: Common or vernacular names of species and substances, especially when given alongside or as an alternative to a scientific or technical name (after "also known as", "or", or in parentheses after a Latin binomial, e.g. Large White, golden orfe, Early Bumble bee). Activation is strongest on the descriptive modifier words of the common name (colour, size, place) and on the connectors that introduce it.

Tokens that begin or form part of common, vernacular names of species and other entities, especially plants and animals, often given next to a scientific name or in lists of alternative names (e.g. "known as", "including"). Activation is strongest on descriptive modifiers such as place, color, or shape words ("Rocky Mountain", "long-finned", "mountain beech") and on the separators that introduce a new common name.

Common (vernacular) names of species, mostly plants and animals, and similar named varieties. It fires on the descriptive modifier words of the name (colors, places, body-part terms such as 'three-toed', 'whitetip', 'cranberry white') and on the connectors that introduce or list them ('known as', 'the', 'and', commas), often next to scientific binomials. It peaks in lists of several species or alternate names.

60081.name: A diffuse feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires weakly on scattered, hard-to-predict tokens. It is strongest in noisy or mixed text such as garbled or mojibake characters, random URL or email fragments, mixed scripts and odd name pieces. It also fires at phrase or segment boundaries, like the first word after punctuation or a list marker, or a function word introducing a new noun phrase.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires near discourse boundaries in scraped web text. It peaks on the opening words of a new segment after a break: a new paragraph, header, caption, signature line or URL boundary. Examples include "Photos:", "Hotel features (", "MADNESS! A recurring", "*The" and "On behalf of". It also fires on the first content words that introduce a new topic or statement, with low activation elsewhere.

60315.name: The word "cut" and its inflections (cuts, cutting, Cut) in any sense: literal slicing, reducing costs or amounts, phrasal verbs (cut off/down/back), idioms (cutting-edge, cut corners), and even as part of names or compounds.

The word "cut" in any form (cut, cuts, cutting, Cut, CUT, -cut), whether literal (slicing, cutting out) or figurative (budget cuts, cut short, cut back, cutting-edge, cut through, cut to the chase). Activation is strongest on verb uses meaning reduce or stop and on idioms, and somewhat lower on 'cutting-edge' and literal slicing.

6036.name: Final subword pieces of proper names, especially author surnames and given names in author or citation lists (often followed by an affiliation number, comma or initial). Weaker activation falls on name-like endings in URLs and sources (".com") and on separators that end an entry, such as a comma, colon or paragraph break.

Fires on the token that completes a multi-token word or entity, most often the final subword piece of a person's name (surname or given name fragments like "eson", "gens", "uger", "ana"). It also fires on endings of other proper nouns, URLs, IDs and number strings. Weaker activations land on sentence-final periods or other tokens that close a unit just before a break such as a newline, citation or "Read More".

6038.name: Words about renting, leasing, and temporary use or access to property and services. It is strongest on "rent" and "rent out", then "leasing", with weaker activation on related terms like lend, borrow, subscribe, own, vacancies, occupied, as-a-service and per month.

Words about renting, leasing, and temporary use of property or services. Rent/rental terms fire strongest, followed by lodging and booking words (hotel, booking, reservation, check-in, stay), lending and borrowing, and housing units. Weaker activations come from related service and transaction terms such as hiring, repair, licensing and providers.

60566.name: The first token (subword fragment) of a multi-token proper name, typically a person's surname or given name (e.g. "Yak" in Yakaboski, "Fe" in Feustel, "Mark" in Markle), activating at the start of the name when it is being split into pieces. The strongest firing is on unusual or foreign names and on repeated mentions. It occasionally fires weakly on other word-initial fragments or ordinary words.

The first token or fragment of a proper name, mostly surnames of people, but also teams, places, products, split into subword pieces. It usually appears where the name is predictable from earlier context, often a repeat mention of an established subject.

60875.name: Expressions of possibility or potential: modal verbs (can, may, could, might) and the verbs/words right after them, along with words like "possible", "possibility that", "potential existence of", "in principle", that mark a hypothetical or capable outcome rather than a definite fact.

Expressions of possibility or potential: modal verbs (can, could, may, might, should) and the verbs right after them (be, happen, cause, occur), plus words like "possible", "possibility", "potentially", "theoretically" and upper-bound phrases ("up to"). Together they mark hypothetical or potential outcomes rather than definite facts.

60886.name: Weak, diffuse feature that fires in contexts of gathering or presenting people's perspectives, accounts and contributions: groups of people consulted, interviewed, invited, or featured (family, aficionados, founders, authors in this volume, members, professionals, artists), plus words for their testimony or output (eyewitness accounts, stories, reactions, proposals, anecdotal reports) and the surrounding function words or verbs (interview, asking, invited, highlight, reviews).

Words that set up reported speech or interviews, where someone is spoken to, interviewed or quoted: "spoke to", "interviewed … about", "said", "admitted on camera", "meet with experts", and opinion or testimonial headers such as "Voices:", "TESTIMONIALS", "Experts Weigh In" and "Profile:". Activation is strongest on "interviewed" and "We spoke to", and also falls on the sentence breaks just before such quotes.

6132.name: Fires mainly on terms from endocrinology and physiology, most strongly on hormones and hormone-related words (estrogens, testosterone, hormone balance, hypothyroid, menstruation, glucocorticoids, adrenaline), often on word-piece subtokens. It also responds more weakly to other biomedical or anatomical fragments and to words like moon/lunar and feminine.

Hormone and endocrine terminology (hormone, hormonal, testosterone, thyroid, oxytocin, corticosteroids, T3/T4, HRT), which activates most strongly. Weaker activations come from loosely related concepts like femininity and masculinity, the moon or lunar cycles, goddesses, birth control, and body or medical terms.

61429.name: Function words (prepositions, articles, conjunctions, commas, list/example introducers like "such as", "like", "include") placed right before an upcoming content noun or name, i.e., the connective slot where the model predicts a specific entity, example item, or list member. Highest on example-introducing words ("like", "such as", "include") and "of" in noun phrases.

Function words (mostly prepositions like of/by/with/in/to, plus articles, 'and', and list commas) that introduce an upcoming noun phrase, typically a named entity, place, or descriptive complement in factual, encyclopedic or product-description prose; activation is on the connector just before the noun, strongest in dense descriptive lists or biographies.

61749.name: The word "month" (and its variants "months", "monthly", "Month") as a time-unit noun, most strongly in singular references to a specific or recurring month ("last month", "this month", "every month", "per month"). Plural counts ("three months", "months ago") and other time units like week, day and hour activate more weakly.

The word "month" (and variants like months, monthly, Month) as a time unit, especially singular "month" in relative time phrases like "last/this/earlier this month" or "per month"; weaker on plural "months" and other time units (weeks, hour, tomorrow).

61949.name: A weak, diffuse feature with no clear semantic focus. It fires mostly on tokens in structured or formatted text: code syntax (brackets, colons, assignments, indentation), markup and citation fields, and section-like headers such as "Media Contact" or "Company Description". It is often near line breaks or the start of a new segment, with only scattered firing on ordinary prose.

A weak, diffuse feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires mostly on highly predictable, low-surprisal tokens in formulaic contexts: the completion of set phrases ("not to mention", "Bill of Rights", "Email Address", "hello-world", "Step 1"). It also fires on boilerplate web text and on structural or syntax tokens in code, HTML and URLs ("https", "<div", "main ()", ";", "time.sleep"), and on line breaks after headers or names. The strongest activations are on code and markup syntax.

61956.name: The final digit of a four-digit year, split as a three-digit prefix plus one digit, especially when it marks the date of a work's publication, release, or founding (often in parentheses after a title or citation).

The final digit of a four-digit year, mostly in release, publication, or creation dates for works such as films, books, and albums. It fires most strongly on years in parentheses after a title or citation. A few weaker hits land on other date-like tokens such as "March" and "this year".

6203.name: Words completing a description of a person's or thing's age, most strongly "old"/"-old" after a number plus "year(s)" (e.g. "26-year-old", "ten years old"). Weaker on other age words (young, teenage, elderly, born) and on similar measurement completions after a number and unit, such as "long", "distant", "enough".

Words that complete descriptors of age or life stage, chiefly "old"/"-old" after a number plus "year(s)" (e.g. "17-year-old", "12 year old"). Weaker hits are other attributive modifiers that characterize a person or thing, such as "-based", "-century", "aged", "underage", "student", "toddler" and "newborn".

Tokens that complete a descriptive modifier placed before or right after a person or thing, mainly age expressions ("-old" in "X-year-old", "years old", the comma after an age in "Smith, 52,"). Weaker activations come from similar compound or attributive descriptors such as "-based", "-long", "-winning", "-era", "graduate students" and "young". The strongest activations are on "-old" in hyphenated ages describing a person.

62069.name: A weak, diffuse feature on nouns, often word-final subword pieces, naming concrete figures or depicted things, especially representations rather than real objects. Typical cases are characters, creatures and objects shown in artwork, emblems, decorations, toys or fiction: the eagle, arrows and stars of a national seal, the Great Wave, mechanical skeletons and a projected witch, a cardboard traffic policeman, miniature aeroplanes, a raven, a ghostly piper, teddy bears and Star Wars. Activation is strongest on such figurative or depicted figures.

Nouns (and suffixes like "-shaped") naming the visual subject, motif or theme of a depicted design: shapes, characters, mascots and icons shown on products, costumes, cakes, patterns, images or artwork. Examples include Batman, hidden Mickeys, heart-shaped cakes, cloud images, flags, seals and camouflage. Activations are mostly weak and diffuse, peaking on character and shape motifs.

62123.name: Continuation tokens that finish a proper name, mostly an organization, company, brand or product name (sometimes a person's name). The token is usually a later subword or word, e.g. a suffix piece like "tran" in Deltran or "Press" in Guilford Press. It fires most strongly on names that repeat in the text.

Non-initial tokens inside proper names, mostly brands, companies, organizations and acronyms (e.g. word-piece endings like 'cker', 'iac', 'ity', or later words like 'Clinic', 'Academy'). They fire on the token that continues or completes the name, not its first piece.

62499.name: Legislative leadership and political power roles, firing most strongly on presiding or leading positions in a legislature (Speaker, Speaker of the House, Majority Leader) and the names of people holding them. It responds more weakly to related government vocabulary: party and coalition leaders, politicians' surnames, Congress, constitution, branch, power, and 'led'/'presided'.

Political and legislative leadership terms, mostly titles and roles like "Speaker", "Majority Leader", "President", "Chairman" and "leadership". These often follow an institution name (House, Senate, Council) and come before a politician's name, which is sometimes also marked. Weaker activations cover other governance vocabulary such as parties, majority, coalition, government formation, factions and support. Activation is strongest on "House Speaker" and "Senate Majority Leader".

62567.name: Fires on the word "definition" or "definitions" in any capitalization or context: dictionary or glossary headings, formal or mathematical definitions, and code definitions such as class, function or type definitions. It is strongest in programming and technical contexts. It fires weakly on related words like "meanings", "creator" and "TypeDef".

The word "definition" or "definitions" in any casing and sense (meaning of a term, section headings, programming declarations, image or sound sharpness). It also fires on related tokens such as "Def" and "typedef", and weakly on "blueprint".

62595.name: Words expressing refutation, contradiction, denial or negation of claims, ideas or laws (rebut, debunk, contradict, repeal, deny, dispute, reject, veto, critique). Strongest on rebutting/debunking/contradicting arguments.

Words that express contradicting, refuting, negating or opposing something, such as a claim, belief, rule or effort (contradict, counter, debunk, dispel, deny, repeal, undermine, negate). They fire most strongly on verbs of refutation that sit right before the thing being opposed.

62626.name: A weak, diffuse feature centered on sentence and segment boundaries in generic web, SEO and marketing text. It fires mostly on sentence-final periods (often followed by a newline or a new topic sentence), on colons and on stray spaces. It also fires weakly on words in headline-like titles (e.g. "Tips", "Start") and on boilerplate UI phrases ("click", "try again", "enter your comment"). One outlier is a strong activation on "you" in an "If you…" clause.

A diffuse, low-level feature that fires on low-quality web text such as SEO/spam articles, article-spinner output, forum and blog boilerplate, and comment spam. It activates most strongly on sentence-final periods followed by line breaks in generic promotional prose, and on odd words in garbled spam ("ebook", "please", "blog ("). Elsewhere it gives scattered weak hits on boilerplate tokens like "post", "read more" and ":".

62706.name: Words describing operations or changes applied to something (replace, add/remove, rearrange, transform, switch, double, modify, tilt, increase), plus the context of whether a result is invariant to or depends on such changes (e.g., "invariant with respect to the renormalization group", "depend on the choice of"). The feature is mostly in technical or mathematical writing and fires weakly on scattered tokens elsewhere.

Words about altering, transforming or freely choosing things: change, transform, deform, move, substitute, transpose, double, cut. It also covers arbitrariness or interchangeability ('any other', 'any two', 'either way', 'same thing on both sides', 'commutative', 'isomorphic'). The shared idea is applying an operation or variation and asking whether the result stays equivalent or invariant. It is strongest in mathematical contexts about equivalence under transformation.

62799.name: Subword fragments in the middle of rare, unfamiliar words, mostly foreign proper names (people, places, companies) and drug names, where a word is split into several uncommon pieces; the activation is on an internal fragment, before the word is finished.

Middle subword fragments inside rare, multi-token proper nouns (mostly unusual surnames, foreign given names, and place names), firing on the internal pieces after the first token and before the word ends.

6283.name: The final noun (or noun phrase) of a coordinated list or conjunction, mostly the item right after "and"/"or" or a list comma that closes the phrase, typically just before a period or comma.

The final noun or noun phrase in a coordinated list or pair, usually right after "and", "or", "but", a comma or "+". It marks the second or later item that completes a parallel series, such as "and Cowboys", "Diplo and Bieber", or "heart, lungs, and brain". Commas or periods that close the item are sometimes included.

62980.name: Words that follow a short imperative verb in website or interface boilerplate, such as "Cite this", "Cite this article as", "Export as", "Share as", "Run as", "Revision as of", "Posting as", "View As". The word "as" after such a command is by far the most frequent, and citation and reference prompts ("Cite this", "cite or link to") activate most strongly.

Function words, chiefly "as" plus "at", "using", "with", "by", that come right after a verb in website boilerplate and UI text, such as "Flag as inappropriate", "Revision as of", "referenced as", "Published at", "Log in using" and "Give as a gift". The words that complete a citation or attribution instruction ("cite the", "Preferred Citation") also activate. In each case the token links an action to the category, format or timestamp that follows it.

6314.name: Tokens inside proper names of places, mostly the later or completing subword piece of a geographic name (city, county, region, district, river, valley). Typical cases are Onondaga, Kitsap, Kingstown, Pradesh and Cape. Activation is weak and also spills onto a few other proper-name fragments, such as person or era names.

Geographic place names (cities, counties, states, regions, countries), with activation mostly on the final or later subword token of the name; strongest on regional/county-level names, especially those followed by words like "County".

63262.name: A weak, diffuse feature found in expository scientific and engineering prose about physical phenomena such as optics, fluids, materials, acoustics and circuits. It fires mostly on structural connectors where the explanation continues: sentence boundaries followed by a new sentence start ('. But', '. A', '. The'), clause commas, parentheses, and prepositions or articles like 'of', 'on the', 'that'. Occasionally it fires on technical nouns such as 'behaviour', 'distribution', 'design' and 'scenarios'.

A diffuse, weak feature that fires across expository science and engineering text, such as research summaries, technology descriptions and environmental or physics explanations. It peaks on words that describe how something works, is designed or is studied: method and purpose phrases ("using", "so that", "to enhance", "included replacing", "aims at studying concepts to"), mechanism nouns ("noise reduction", "charge modulation") and fragments of technical names.

64245.name: Words that express opposition or being against something, e.g. "oppose/opposed/opposing", "opposition (to)", "opponents of", "against", along with weaker antonymic or obstructive relations ("antithetical to", "obstructed", "in favor"). The strongest activations fall on forms of "oppose".

Words expressing opposition or a stance against something (oppose/opposed/opposing, against, opponents, opposition, at odds, object to), with the strongest activations on verbs like "opposed". Weaker activations appear on support or favor terms (support, favor, backs, all for) and on "opp" letter strings in unrelated words (Oppenheimer, Stoppard, oppression).

64251.name: Mostly numeric tokens in sequences or references: list/part numbers, citation superscripts, page numbers, years' final digits, dates and counts. These are often items in an ordered series (Part 8, 9, 10…; refs 16, 17). Weaker activation on sentence-ending periods/paragraph breaks and a few ordinal words ("second", "five").

Numbers (or the final digit/ordinal suffix of a number) that act as an identifier in a sequence or index: dates (day after a month, last digit of a year), citation/figure/item/issue numbers, "N of M" counters, list numbering and ordinals. Month names that precede a date also activate weakly.

64707.name: Words that introduce source attribution, citation or provenance information: e.g. "quoted in/by", "reprinted", "reproduced", "posted", "retrieved from", "via", "licensed under", "Wikimedia/Commons", "see", "author of". They usually follow a source name or comma in credits, bylines and references. Strongest on "quoted"; weak, scattered activation on other connective words.

Words in attribution, sourcing and provenance phrases, mostly passive verbs and prepositions saying where content was published, quoted, credited, found or distributed (e.g. via, quoted by, published, posted, seen, referred to, Associated Press, License Photo, Supported by). Strongest on 'via' and 'quoted by'.

64717.name: First names or initials of people, mostly in author/contributor lists (academic papers, bylines), with the strongest activation on given names that come after the first entry in a list of several people and sit just before the surname.

First names (or their first subword/initial token) of people, especially a second or later person in a list of authors, researchers or credited contributors (after commas, "and", "Dr.", or a line break), usually followed by a surname and affiliation.

64787.name: Tokens that open a variable placeholder or interpolation in code, shell commands, URLs, or templates, such as "(!" field references, "${", "={", "{{", "%" format specifiers, and "$". These are the positions where a variable name or value gets substituted into a string or expression. Much weaker activations occur on scattered ordinary tokens, notably "page" in the boilerplate "top of page".

Template placeholders and variable slots: the opening delimiters ({{, {, [[, [, <, $) and names of fill-in fields where text is meant to be substituted (e.g. {{amount}}, {table_name}, <name>, [post_name], [insert ...], $search). It fires most strongly on the opening bracket of these slots and also weakly on other code-like syntax and odd fill-in tokens.

64872.name: Diffuse, mostly weak activations in expository technical writing, mainly programming, math and software docs. They fire on words that define or describe an abstract entity and how it is referenced, passed or made available, e.g. "is an object", "available to your scripts as the context object", "a symbol (like x, y, or z)", variables, placeholders, arrays and values. The strongest hits fall on explanations of what an identifier or object represents.

Mostly technical/programming documentation describing what role an entity plays or where it goes, such as how a value is passed, represented, added or placed. It fires most on role nouns like 'argument', 'variables', 'parameter', 'Context', 'slots' and 'pronoun', and on role-assigning phrases like 'passed as the first argument', 'is represented by a' and 'added as a'. It also fires weakly on placeholder-like tokens such as 'None' and 'XXXX'.

649.name: Diffuse, low-level activation across tokens of generic, formulaic web prose, strongest and densest in SEO/marketing-style or boilerplate explanatory text (e.g., product pitches, business advice, health claims), with weaker spikes at sentence boundaries and transitional phrases (". This", "In fact", "Moreover"). Specific narrative or news content activates only sparsely.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires broadly on ordinary tokens (content nouns, verbs, connectives, punctuation) in generic expository or assistant-style text, such as tech and code explanations, tutorials, product descriptions, and essays, including garbled or non-English text. It has no specific lexical trigger. It peaks mildly on runs of descriptive or explanatory prose, for example marketing claims like 'boxes are both durable and safe'.

65114.name: Forms of the word "disclose" (disclose, disclosed, disclosure(s), undisclosed, and the "losure" piece of non-disclosure) in any sense: revealing information, legal or financial disclosure, and affiliate disclaimers. Weak activations appear on related revealing verbs such as "divulge" and "discussed".
Forms of the word "disclose" (disclose, disclosed, disclosure(s), undisclosed, Disclosure headers), i.e., revealing or making information known; weakly also fires on the similar-looking "discourse".

65400.name: The first symbol or token after an equals sign (or similar relation) in math, physics or code expressions, firing most strongly when the right-hand side repeats the variable or function name from the left side (e.g. u(0,x)=u(x), V=V_per+V_ω, ξ=ξ_S, f(x)=f(0)+…, y(0)=y(h), dp[i]=dp[…]).

The first token(s) on the right-hand side of a mathematical equation or definition (right after "=" or another relation), firing hardest when that symbol repeats the variable or function named on the left (e.g. "u = u(x,t)", "W = WΦ", "a = a'"). It fires weakly on similar relational slots in prose and code.

Math/code variables at the start of an expression's right-hand side (just after '=' or a relation), especially when they repeat a symbol from the left side, as in v = v_0 or f(a) = f(b). More weakly, any token that copies an earlier word or identifier (sacrificed the sacrifice, mute/unmute, repeated function names in code).

6647.name: The conditional keyword "if"/"If" that begins a condition, strongest in code if-statements (e.g. "if (" / "if ($") and also common in sentence-initial prose "If" clauses. Weaker activation spreads onto the tokens of the condition expression, with faint scattered hits on other tokens.

Words opening a conditional clause, mainly sentence-initial "If"/"if" (also "Should", or a bare condition after "If"), especially when they lead into a branch or alternative outcome such as "If not…" or "if unsuccessful…". The pattern extends to comparison and condition operators in code ("!==", "<", "=").

670.name: A weak, diffuse feature firing on the opening words of a new sentence, title, or clause, often right after a heading or paragraph break. It covers the framing lead-in (subject, verb, and function words such as "I believe that if you want to", "Those who want to", "The funny thing is,", "Know Your Credit") up to, but usually not including, the main content noun.

A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires across stretches of ordinary running prose (function words, verbs, noun phrases mid-clause) rather than on specific tokens. It is strongest within explanatory or narrative clauses and is common in noisy, incoherent, or machine-generated-looking text, including prose fragments mixed into code or web boilerplate.

6780.name: Clause or sentence boundaries, mostly the period (or period plus newline) ending a sentence and sometimes the first word of the next sentence, plus commas, semicolons and parentheses that close a clause. The strongest firing is on a sentence-final period after a completed statement, especially where the text continues with a new sentence.

Sentence and clause boundaries: mostly the period (or other end punctuation, often with following newlines) that closes a complete statement, plus clause-joining commas and conjunctions ("and", "while", "though", "But", "And") where one idea ends and the next begins. Activation is strongest at the end of short factual or listing statements.

6887.name: The second element of a hyphenated compound modifier (e.g., "-solving", "-energy", "-gas", "-quality"), i.e., the hyphen-prefixed token joining a word to the preceding word to form a compound adjective/noun modifier, usually before a head noun; weak scattered activations on other modifiers.

Tokens that join a word to the noun or word it modifies, mostly hyphenated compound pieces ("-meter", "-end", "-hour", "-abuse") forming compound modifiers. Possessive apostrophes ("trainers'", "day’s") also fire because they link a possessor to the following noun.

6889.name: Weak, diffuse feature that fires most on words expressing equivalence, sameness or correspondence between things (equivalent, equal to, synonyms, identical, interchangeable, comparable, proportional, mappings, transformation, rename). It also gives faint activations on scattered word fragments and technical terms.

Words expressing sameness, equivalence or similarity between things (equivalent, same, isomorphism, synonyms, similarities, tantamount, twin, homogeneous, interchangeably, "amount to"), strongest on "isomorphism"; other activations are weak and scattered.

70.name: The very first token of a document, whatever it is (a title word, heading, byline, navigation text, newline or whitespace), marking the start of the text.

Fires on the very first token of a document or text sequence, whatever that token happens to be (a word, word fragment, symbol, code keyword, or whitespace/newline). Where the text opens with repeated filler like newlines or asterisks, the leading run is marked as well. The feature tracks sequence-start position, not content.

700.name: A broad, diffuse activation over ordinary running text: it covers long stretches of fluent prose, mostly in mid-sentence descriptive or explanatory clauses (marketing copy, narration, technical how-to). Activation tends to rise toward content words late in the clause. It is weaker or absent on code, boilerplate and identifiers, and is not tied to specific words.

A diffuse, weakly firing feature that spans runs of substantive content tokens in LLM/assistant-style technical text, such as code and markup, math formulas and worked calculations, problem statements, and clarification requests. It does not single out one specific word, and it is strongest on the core phrase of an explanation or definition.

7555.name: Weak, diffuse activations on tokens that cite or attribute information to media and publication sources: news articles, journals, press and source lines, URLs (https://www…), bylines, transcripts, interviews and 'according to'/'told'/'said' attributions.

Language about news media and the sourcing or attribution of reported information: news outlets and press items (news, media, press release/conference, story, edition, report, interview), attribution phrases ("according to", "reports say", "as the Guardian reports", "courtesy of", "via the", "photo credit"), and the punctuation or byline points where such a citation would begin or end.

7700.name: The token "ion" as a standalone word or word piece in physics/chemistry terms (ion, ions, ionic, ionization, ionosphere, deionized), plus related charged-particle vocabulary (electrolyte, plasma, charged particle, proton, salt). Weaker matches come from unrelated words that merely contain "ion" or similar pieces, such as Deion, Hyperion and SERMION.

Mainly the token "ion"/"Ion" in any setting: chemistry and physics (ions, ionized, lithium ion, Ionosphere) as well as unrelated words containing it (Ionian Sea, Saturn Ion, Psion, Hyperion). Activation is weaker on related charged-particle or chemistry vocabulary (salts, electrolytes, particles, plasma, rays, radical, charged) and on look-alike fragments such as "lion", "aura" and "desal(ination)".

790.name: Phrases that introduce the contrasting or alternative counterpart in a comparison, e.g. after 'but', 'however', 'on the other hand', 'while', 'instead', 'in contrast to' or 'else'. The activation spans the second side of the opposition (symmetric vs asymmetric, junior vs senior, metal vs asphalt, responders vs non-responders, autoflowers vs photoperiods), including code branches like 'else' or 'rest'.

Weak, diffuse activation, mostly in technical, coding or explanatory text. It fires on phrases that set up a contrasting or alternative case against something stated just before. Typical triggers are words like "otherwise", "instead", "but here" and "usually". Examples include "with let, the value can be changed" after a const case, a modified condition after the original, "the second line has 4 spaces" after the first line, and "became strong" after "weak". Activation is strongest on the key contrasting content words (can, lighter, update, immutable, address).

8207.name: A weak, diffuse feature for chemistry and lab-science language. It fires most strongly in chemistry research abstracts: phrases like "is reported.", reagents, nucleophilic, carbocations, kJ mol units, chemical reactions, and chemistry laboratories. It also fires faintly on a scattering of other technical or scientific tokens, such as units, citations and terms from scientific prose.
The word "chemistry" (and, more weakly, nearby chemistry-related terms like chemical, elements, metal, spill). Other activations are faint and scattered.

842.name: Tokens in the trailing elaboration at the end of a sentence, mostly infinitive purpose clauses ("to help you manage…"), relative clauses ("that could affect…") and prepositional phrases ("for the next generation of…") that extend a statement toward its final noun. Activation usually rises as the phrase approaches the closing period, and the very last word is often not marked.

A diffuse, weak feature on the trailing complement of a clause: the prepositional, infinitival or participial phrase that finishes a predicate (e.g. 'to improve the security', 'for subsequent steps', 'to successfully execute the code'). It fires on the function words and content words inside the phrase, and activation often rises toward the phrase's end, just before punctuation. This is common in technical and instructional text, which is often garbled or machine-generated.

85.name: A diffuse, low-level feature that activates across long runs of ordinary content tokens in factual prose rather than on any specific word. It is strongest in news-style reporting, such as statements of who announced, found or did something, attributions like 'a professor of… at… College', and statistics like '98 live births'. It fires weakly and sporadically on nouns and function words in general expository text, and barely at all in code or metadata.

A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no single clear trigger. It mostly lands on content words (usually nouns, sometimes verbs) that complete a phrase or clause, such as objects, complements and list items before a comma or period. The strongest activations come from descriptive or enumerative passages like item lists, quantities and title or summary headings.

8846.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on head nouns or word-piece continuations that complete multi-token technical terms, compound nouns and proper names, such as instrument and method names, institutions, software and surnames. It is strongest in scientific and technical text, e.g. the second or third part of terms like "Spin Rotation", "Box Score", "X-ray laser" and "Berkeley Mapper".

Weak, diffuse feature that fires on tokens completing a predictable word or fixed phrase: subword continuations of names and technical terms (S-ayers, Ros-etta, Borgh-ese, Bay-esian, Mucolipid-osis, Changes-et, Gnu-PG) and the second element of set compounds or named entities (pattern recognition, reverse engineered, patent prosecution, Press Standards, Proto Labs, AP poll).

8941.name: Phrases that define a target audience or the conditions under which a recommendation applies: who something is for or suits ("for those who…", "for someone who…", "freelancers looking to…", "families with…") and conditional clauses about a reader's preferences, needs or situation ("if you want to…", "if X isn't your thing", "your specific goals and needs"). Activation is generally weak and diffuse.

Conditional or target-audience qualifiers that state when, for whom, or under what circumstances something applies: phrases like "if you want/need…", "when you only have…", "for customers who need…", "in systems where…", and "for projects with…". These typically appear in recommendation or explanatory text, often in technical or assistant-style writing.

924.name: Weak, diffuse activation on tokens inside repetitive, list-like or unstructured text that isn't ordinary prose: number and symbol sequences, code and URL fragments, keyword-stuffed tags, garbled spaced-out letters, line breaks in lists or verse, and math notation. It is strongest on repeated or sequential patterns such as "b b b 1 2 3", strings of underscores and dots, and runs of numbers.

Fires across garbled, nonsensical or highly repetitive token sequences: random symbol/number strings, repeated characters or words, mixed-language gibberish, malformed code and list-like fragments. Activation rises the longer and more patternless or repetitive the noise becomes, and stays low in coherent prose.

9416.name: Code tokens that emit a message: output, error and warning functions or operators (print, puts, printf, println, die, warn, fatalError, qDebug <<) that come right before a quoted string literal. Weaker activations land on miscellaneous tokens before quoted or explanatory text in prose.

Tokens immediately preceding a quoted string or message content, especially output/print calls and constructors in code (new Error(', cout <<, print, println, document.write) and keys/attributes before string values ("title":, title=). It also fires weakly on prose words that introduce communicated content (said X,; let us know; email us with; include your name).

9590.name: A diffuse, low-level feature that fires weakly on scattered mid-sentence tokens, mostly function words, nouns and verbs, in technical, instructional or explanatory prose. It is strongest inside code and formula syntax, such as function calls, parentheses, '#(' and 'sqrt(points', where the next tokens follow predictably from structure.

A diffuse, low-intensity pattern with no clear semantic theme. The strongest common thread is tokens that complete a predictable collocation or word given the preceding context: the noun after a modifier (plain flour, cell phone, set an alarm, Pillsbury biscuits), the second half of a set phrase (Terms and Concepts, Asia-Pacific), the verb after a modal (must place, have to win and), or a word-final subword (mathematic-ian, Gigg-les). Isolated stronger hits occur on regex bracket syntax.

9807.name: Weak, diffuse feature that fires on words about physical parts, surfaces and contact or attachment between things. Typical hits are body or object parts and surfaces (bone, arms, fingernail, buckle, cursor, shoes, pockets, surface). It also catches attaching or contact verbs and the prepositions after them (attached to the, connected to, cling to, bite into, docked to, fit seamlessly with). A similar 'X linked to / value of Y' relation in code or API text (page_token must be the value of next_page_token) also activates it.

A weak, diffuse pattern centered on physical contact and spatial placement. It fires mostly on concrete nouns for body parts, object parts or surfaces (foot, elbow, shoulder, skin, side, back, chamber, banister, floor). It also fires on the prepositional phrases that locate or attach something to them ("on the top of the", "to the stone floor", "attached to the appropriate devices", "into the side of"). The strongest activations come in descriptions of something being placed on, pressed against or fastened to a surface.

982.name: Tokens that repeat or continue a pattern just established in the context: duplicated words or phrases ("cries and cries", "unite, unite", "many, many", "oh, oh", "end goal after the end goal"), runs of the same symbol or character ("- - - -", dot leaders, "9999", "WOOOOO"), and parallel list or sequence items (page numbers 1 2 3, "45µl, 55µl", "H + H", "\cdot"). Activation is strongest on clear repeats of a preceding token.

Tokens inside repetitive or predictable sequences: repeated symbols, numbers, words, or code fragments (e.g. "// // //", "1 1 1", "bodybody", "20-20-", backtick runs). Activation grows as the repetition continues, and there is weaker activation on simple continuations like counting lists.

983.name: Function words and connective glue, such as prepositions (of, to, in, for, between), articles (the, a), conjunctions (and, or, that) and commas. They fire most where a word is about to be followed by a noun phrase or complement, as in "using the", "use the" and "discussion of". This is a broad syntactic signal for introducing an upcoming object or argument rather than anything tied to meaning.

A diffuse feature with no single trigger word. It fires mostly on function words inside running prose that link one phrase to the next, especially "of", "the", "and", "to", "in", "with" and "by". Activation peaks on "of" in phrases like "effects of", "idea of" and "construction of a". Some content words also light up, mainly verbs and modifiers that set up a following phrase ("reducing", "activate", "implement"). It fires weakly on the analogous connecting symbols in code, lists and markup, such as "->", "=", bullets and list numbering.

9895.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on structural boundary tokens, where one unit ends and the next begins. These include sentence- and clause-ending punctuation (commas, periods followed by newlines) and line breaks. Its strongest activations are on code statement delimiters and connectors (braces, semicolons, 'or die', '&&', '->__', '())') and on transitions from prose into code. It also fires on short header or label words in web and page layouts.

Tokens at the boundary just before reported speech or program output, typically the punctuation, speaker name or pronoun that comes right before a speech verb or quotation (e.g. '...daughters, Obama said', 'He said, “...”', 'Mr. Trump tweeted:'). In code, the same thing happens around print and output statements and the closing of their strings (") ;", ")//").

991.name: Words naming a role, office, or job title, especially leadership, management, or authority positions (director, manager, president, chair, CEO, mayor), often with a following "of"/"in". Weaker hits on management/administration words and on organizational or academic units.

Job titles, offices and roles held by people (president, director, VP of, head of, mayor, editor, CEO, adviser to), usually in appositive or descriptive phrases identifying someone's position. The strongest activations come on senior or leadership titles, often including the trailing "of"/"to".

996.name: A diffuse, low-intensity signal spread over long runs of ordinary prose in polished, expository or narrative writing (journalism, essays, marketing, fiction) and not tied to any specific word. It is strongest on wordy descriptive or rhetorical clauses, such as "would make history as the world's first," "a restful night's sleep is the foundation of," or "It is seamless, whole and complete." It is weak on isolated words and on proper names, numbers and list-like text.

A diffuse, weak feature that fires across spans of fluent, formulaic prose, strongest on mid-clause continuation words in generic, cliché, LLM-style phrasing such as stock narrative, marketing, advice or explanatory sentences (e.g. 'demand has been steadily rising', 'don't be afraid to think creatively', 'make every interaction effortless'). It fires only sporadically and weakly on isolated tokens in garbled or code-like text.

999.name: Tokens right before a capitalized word, usually a proper noun, personal name, brand or acronym (e.g. 'to' before Okta, 'from' before Mary Cassatt, 'Dr.' before Brei). Also name fragments mid-name ('Shish|u Qu', 'Rus|son Gilman'), and breaks, colons or bullets that start a new capitalized line or item.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires mostly on function words, punctuation and line breaks immediately before an upcoming proper noun or named entity, such as a brand, product, organization, team, person or place (e.g. 'in' before a place name, ', a spokeswoman for' before an airline, '.⏎⏎' before a product title). It also fires on early or partial tokens inside such names. In effect it anticipates that a capitalized name is coming next.
